speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in committee on Bill (No. 88) to provide for the appointment of a Tariff Commission.
On section 5, subsection 7-inquiries to be in Ottawa, but power to hold them elsewhere.

I desire to_ point out what I conceive to be a defect in the machinery provided: for the purpose of obtaining information of parties who may be prepared to give testimony before the commission.
I pointed out before that this clause provides for the examination of such persons only, who have been summoned for the purpose of giving evidence. I think this clause should go further and provide for the examination of any person who is willing to go before the commission -to represent any interest in Canada, whether he has been summoned or not. With that view, I propose that section 5, subsection 1, he amended by adding at the end thereof the following words:-
And they shall hear the evidence of persons who appear before them for the purpose of making a voluntary statement and who have not been so summoned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it should be borne in mind that this commission _ is to be used for the purpose of obtaining information, and to be used intelligently, under the direction of the government. The amendment would very seriously interfere with the action of the commission in that respect. Under section 4 it is provided that the commission is to act under the direction of the Minister of Finance; and it has been .previously pointed out that it will be asked to r.eport upon certain matters in the order oif their urgency as it appears to the government. In order to take up its work'intelligently, the commission must be at liberty to direct its own operations, to summon witneses if they wish, or to allow parties to be heard. I think that if my hon. friend (Mr. Kyte) will look at the provision of the Act creating the Railway Commission, he will find that no one has the right to come and ask that the commission take up a. certain matter. That.

is for the commission to decide. Otherwise the commission, instead of working intelligently, would he art the heck and call of every one who wished to have his particular matter taken up, even though entirely out of its order; and the result would be that instead of intelligent action on the part of the commission, more or less confusion would ensue. I think it may be safely left to the commission appointed1 by the government, the commissioners, we may assume, will be men of intelligence- to adopt their own methods of obtaining evidence, either by summoning witnesses, or by affording opportunity for parties who wish to be heard to come forward and testify. The last clause of the last subsection of section 5, appears to cover the point raised by my hon. friend.
The commissioners shall hold their sessions and conduct their proceedings in suoh manner as may seem to them most convenient for the speedy and efficient discharge of their duties.
In pursuing a certain inquiry it is open to the commission to say that all parties who desire to do so may appear, or they may subpoena witnesses on their own initiative. I have no reason to doubt that they will hear interested panties' who desire to be heard on any particular inquiry, but the initiative should be with them, in order, that, as I have said, they may conduct their work with the greatest efficiency and intelligence. But to adopt the amendment of my hon. friend would mean that the work of the commission might be very greatly embarrassed, and we should not be able to accomplish through the commission what we hope to accomplish, namely to obtain information -connected with tariff matters required from time to time by the government.
If I may hark back to the discussion of last evening, I would like to add that the time when we shall need the reports of the commission most will- be between sessions. It is almost impossible for a government or a minister to consider such important matters as the tariff, and especially tariff changes, during a busy session. The time when such matters should be most particularly considered is between sessions. That is a little apart from the amendment, but I thought it desirable to point it out as it was overlooked by me in dealing with the matter before.
I have no reason to doubt that in practice what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kyte) desired will be carried out, but carried out in such order as the commission may deem proper, for the best accomplishment of their work.

In my opinion, if the committee were to adopt the amendment of the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), it would be almost impossible for the commission to conduct any inquiry in, this country without persons coming before the commission, and interfering with the examination of witnesses, and asking the commission to hear any person who
354.3

might offer himself. It might be very well if, after the commission has been at work for some time, there comes a complaint from any portion of the country that the commission had refused, on application, to hear the views of certain persons; then I think perhaps this amendment would be in order, and might be adopted by both sides of the House. This commission is experimental; this is the first time in the history of Canada that we have [DOT] had a commission of this kind, and I think it would be in the public interest that hon. gentlemen opposite should give it a fair trial. Surely the Finance Minister sand the government w<ll make every effort to investigate every tariff question thoroughly; the government will be more anxious than any one else that such should be done. Any person who has a statement to make to the government can come before the government at any time, and make an appointment with the Minister of Finance with respect to tariff matters, and it will be the duty of the minister to hear that complaint, no matter from what part of Canada it may come. I cannot see that this amendment would be good. I think the commission would be quite willing to hear any person, and the government would naturally be anxious that every person should be heard who desired to be heard, no matter from what part of the country he may come. Suppose a day was fixed by the commission for sitting in Toronto to hear a certain matter; under the Bill as it now stands, certain persons would be summoned, and men will understand that they are to come and give evidence. If this amendment were adopted, any persons would have a right to come in and demand that the commission should hear them. If next week, or ten days after, the commission should have an appointment at Hamilton on their route, it would be absolutely impossible for them, under the operation of this amendment, to meet their appointment, or to carry out any general investigation of tariff matters, beginning at one city and going on to another, because the public would crowd in and interfere with their arrangements. It would be the next thing to impossible to give everybody who wished an opportunity of being heard before the commission on any fixed date. Surely this is asking the government to throw the door open too wide. 1 repeat that if, in the future, it is found that tne commissioners are unwilling to hear complaints, and if a complaint is made to the House, I am sure that the government will be quite ready to amend the Act, or make some regulation by which everybody may have an opportunity to state his grievance. For my part I think the amendment is out of Mr. BLAIN.
order, and I would like to ask the chairman whether it is or not.

In the case of members of the government who have been acting as commissioners with respect to tariff matters, and who, when they come to any city, have invited all persons who desire to appear before them and give evidence, has the hon. gentleman ever heard of any inconvenience arising by reason of the public crowding in?

I cannot say offhand. I do know, however, that the other day we heard a gentleman, who was a member of a former government and a member of this government, saying that he had been one of a committee that had traversed the country to hear complaints, and that when he came back he did not know any more about the matter than before he went away.
Probably lie had not studied the evidence.

I think my hon. friend will agree that he was a gentleman who would have studied the evidence pretty carefully. I do not think that the mover of this amendment should introduce it at this stage, at the very inception of the Tariff Commission. I think it would be in the interest of the public if he would give the commission opportunity of getting into operation; and then, if he finds them failing in the discharge of their duty, an amendment of this kind might be proper.

Notwithstanding the appeal of my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain),
I am still of the opinion that the amendment which I have proposed is an eminently proper one. My hon. friend states two objections. One is that it might lead to parties coming in and interfering with the commission, interfering with the line of conduct which they have laid down to guide them in particular instances. I understand that this commission will be in the nature of a court, it will have power to regulate the attendance of witnesses and the hearing of testimony, and like any other court, it would have a right to restrict the number of witnesses who might appear for the _ purpose of giving testimony upon a particular point.
Not according to my hon. friend's amendment.

I think so. I think the commissioners, being gentlemen of common sense and familiar with the manner in which inquiries of this kind are carried on, would see to it that no undue advantage was taken of the commission by any persons, and that no waste of time

should occur by going over the same class of evidence the second time.
How could they so regulate proceedings if the amendment were adopted?
If my amendment is not carried, people may not appear, as a right, before the commission at all. So far there are two evils, I think the amendment is in the direction of the lesser evil.
Has my hon. friend in his mind that the commission will be unwilling to hear complaints?

I would be sorry to come to that conclusion; but I must confess, in view of certain statemieaitis made by hon. gentlemen opposite, that I am afraid there will not be too great an eagerness on the part of the commission to hear certain representations that might be offered. My hon. friend also objected to my amendment because it would be throwing the door open too wide. That is exactly the difficulty hon. gentlemen opposite seem to have; they don't want to open the door wide enough to allow all persons in this community to represent their views on tariff questions.
What class of persons has my hon. friend in mind that the commission would be unwilling to hear?

My amendment covers all classes in the community, and in that ' respect it is not too wide. I can imagine circumstances under which the commissioners might go to certain places for the purpose of taking testimony, and when they might or might not desire to hear certain persons who wished to be heard. I suppose that the commission, before leaving Ottawa, will map out a certain itinerary, will select certain places where they will go to hear testimony. They will go down to Halifax, for instance, and certain persons there will be notified of their coming, and may be summoned to appear before the commission. Certain other persons who would like to put their views before the commission on tariff matters might not be able to appear'before the commission.
It will be impossible that -the commission should have in mind every interest in a large community that might desire to go before the commission and present their views. _ No harm can possibly come to the operation of this Act if the amendment is accepted. It will relieve the commission of the charge that might hereafter be made against them of having purposely omitted to notify certain persons or certain interests in the community that they are visiting for the purpose of taking testimony. The regulation of the conduct of the commission will be entirely in their own hands and, as I stated in the beginning, no disorder would be felt from this because the commission will have absolute power to make regulations for their conduct and for carrying out the course which they have laid down for themselves. Therefore, the objection of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), I think, should not prevail because this commission will have power to prevent any unnecessary interference with the business that would properly come before them.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kyte) intend to put it beyond the control of the commission entirely as to the number of persons who shall give evidence or the kind of evidence that shall be given to the commission, because that is the effect of his amendment. There might be a hundred persons who were determined that they should be heard by this commission; the amendment says that they shall be heard and the commission have no power to say that they shall not, or to judge of the kind of evidence that shall be given, but these people simply come there, a hundred in number, and say: We must be heard, irrespective of whether the evidence shall be advisable or pertinent to the question at issue. Does the hon. gentleman want to put the commission in the position that these people shall have the absolute right to come before them and sly: We are going to give this evidence; we do not care what anybody does or whether it is relevant to the question or not. That is the effect of the amendment proposed by the hon. gentleman. The commission have absolute authority to receive the evidence of anybody who has been subpoenaed both under section 5 and subsection 8 of section 5. If that authority is given to the commission surely they would not prevent evidence being given which was pertinent or proper. If they would I would say that, the commission would be no use whatever and would not be doing their duty. I cannot believe that my hon. friend would be willing to force the commission into the position which I have described.

I am very much surprised to hear the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) even suggesting that the amendment of my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) should be refused. There has been a suspicion throughout the discussion of this Bill that the commission was appointed for a purpose. If there is anything in the world that would make the public believe that it was appointed for the purpose of serving the high tariff party, the action of the Minister of Finance would confirm them in that belief. The hon. gentleman who just sat down (Mr. Middlebro) and the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) talked about people going
354"

and crowding tlie court room and demanding to be heard. I would like to know what *country we are living in. Is this a free *country? Are we going to appoint an autocratic commission in a democratic country or are the people of this country going to say that they have the right to be heard on a matter of public interest? Does the minister refuse to accept the amendment of my hon. friend which proposes that anybody in this country who desires to go before the Tariff Commission shall be heard? The Minister of Finance said that it was not so with reference to the Railway Commission. The Railway Commission pride themselves on the fact that anybody in this *country, from end to end of it can be heard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This amendment *says that they 1 shall ' hear evidence. Are the Railway Commission really compelled to hear evidence as this amendment proposes?
They do hear it anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Are they compelled to do it?

This commission should be compelled to do it. Who are they anyway? Do they own the country, or do the people of the country own the commission? Why should wre not say that they ahall, I would like to know ? If there is anything in the world that would cause the people to be dissatisfied with this commission and with its star chamber proceedings, it is the stand which the Minister of Finance takes this afternoon. Why should anybody in this country be refused the right to he heard by this commission? They talk about court rooms being crowded. That is all nonsense. Everybody knows that the commission will be tiie judge as to the method and as to the time at which they shall be heard. My hon. friend talks about fair play for the -commission ; there is no man who is going to be so unreasonable that he will not be willing to wait until the time comes for him to be heard, but he wants to be heard and he will see that he does get the Tight to be heard whether it is now or hereafter. Why should he not? Every man in this *country is interested in this Tariff Commission, everybody who buys anything is interested in the tariff, and everybody has the right to he heard. I think the Minister of Finance is standing in his own light in refusing this amendment. I see no Teason why he should not do so, and I hope that he will reconsider his decision. What are the people of this country, that they should be dictated to by a Tariff Commission, as to whether they shall be heard or shall not be heard, on a question that so vitally affects them as the tariff? Why, the thing is ridiculous.
Mr. NESBITT

One of the reasons, it seems to me, why power should still _ reside in the commission to hear or reject evidence, is just because it frequently happens before commissions, in courts of law, and in parliament also, that much that is offered to be said is irrelevant to the question at issue. If the amendment proposed by the hon. memlber for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), should carry, the commission would be robbed of every power which every commission in existence now has, and which the courts of law have as wrelt. The very power which, the hon. gentleman says, resides in the commission is to be taken away by the amendment. Any man, any crank, any enthusiast, any set of people, individually or collectively, could go before the commission and 'be heard for as long, or as short a time as, in their own individual notions they desired. It would really appear to me that the purpose of the hon. gentleman, in wishing to proceed with the amendment, is to defeat the objects of the commission. If the amendment'read with the word ' may ' instead of the word ' shall' then the commission would still have power to regulate their own proceedings, but if the amendment read 1 may ' I do not see *that the Bill, as it now stands, would be affected in any way, because under two clauses of the Bill, the commissioners have power to hear any one. So, it is evident that the word ' shall ' in the amendment alters the effect of the Bill and it would have the effect of destroying the usefulness of the measure altogether. I know of no , way, if the amendment were to carry. in which the commission would have power to reject irrelevant testimony or to determine the time or place at which they would sit.
It would have the effect of .striking out every other clause in the Bill. I am sure that the hon. member for Richmond, on reconsideration, will see that the purpose which he wishes to be served will be destroyed by the introduction of this amendment. The hon. member for Oxford, (Mr. Nesbitt) it seems to me, inadvertently, stumbled on an objection to the amendment. The Railway Commission of Canada to-day is popular because it has adopted the policy of hearing testimony relative to any issue that is within its jurisdiction. Rut. the Railway Act, which constitutes the Railway Commission, will be searched in vain for a clause which compels the Railway Commission to hear anybody and everybody who presents himself nr any subject that he might choose to talk about.
It does not give a procedure to enable anybody to get before that commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly.
This Bill does not.
There is nothing in this Bill to prevent anybody getting before it; the commission is there to hear evidence.

Is there anything in the Bill now before the committee to provide a method by which a person may appear before the Tariff Commission if he wants to ? I do not think there is a clause in the Bill to give any person the right of appearing before the commission.

I do not think there is any clause in the Railway Act giving any person the right to appear before the Railway Commission in so many words, there is no such procedure for getting before the Railway Commission.
The procedure for getting before the Railway Commission is well defined.

I have often had appearances made and all I had to do was to write to the secretary of the Railway Commission and ask to be heard, and the secretary replied appointing a day and a place. That oan be done under this Act in just the same way.

Referring to the illustration of my hon. friend I have never heard of any restriction in the number of witnesses that might be summoned in a case in -a court of law. If they have relevant testimony to give, the court must hear them. The illustration of my hon. friend fails altogether and rather goes to prove the other side of the case, when be brings in a court of law. When the Tariff Commission of the late government visited my town in 1896, they put a notice in the newspapers that they were to hold a. meeting in a certain place at a certain hour, and invited people to go and give their views on all questions under investigation. There was no trouble, the manufacturers and the consumers, any one who had anything to say, went before the commission and had a right to be heard. If, as has been intimated, the commissioners are to be in sympathy with the views of the government, and if the views of the government are in favour of a high tariff, then, if the commissioners wished simply to procure evidence to support the views of one side, they may invite to any sitting as witnesses only those whose views they knew to he in sympathy with What they desired.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not any doubt that the commission will be glad to hear the views of all classes of the community. I agree with my hon. friend that the effect of this amendment would be really to change the purpose that we have in view. It says that they ' shall ' hear the *evidence of persons who appear before
them. That is to say, the control of the proceedings before the commission is taken away from the commissioners themselves, [DOT]and any one who desires may appear before them and keep appearing as long as he chooses, with the result that it would be possible to block the operations of the commission and destroy their usefulness.
Does the minister think that the ordinary public would insist on continuing to appear before the commission in any numbers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, but we are making a law now, and it is not advisable to insert a clause which is mandatory and which may destroy the purpose we have in view and take the control of the procedure before the commission out of the hands of the commissioners.
Why refuse the people's right there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is nothing in this Bill that will prevent the commissioners from taking evidence either on oath or in any other way. That is provided under section 5.

How would it do to say:
The commissioners shall also give reasonable opportunity to persons who may not have been so summoned to appear before them, and give evidence on any matter referring to an inquiry then being made by the commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will consider that, if this section is allowed to stand.
That is free from the objections which have been heard, it only imposes on the commissioners the duty of giving a reasonable opportunity.
Who will define what ' reasonable ' means?
That is in the judgment of the commissioners.
Then why not leave it all to the commissioners ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what we have done.

As the law now stands it would be an impertinence for any one to come before the commissioners without having been summoned. It would be regarded as impertinent and people would not go. The result would be that when the commission would go into a town, they would issue subpoenas to people to come before them; that nobody who had not beeu summoned would think of going before them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would be necessary to change the preceding section if we adopt the amendment suggested by the

lion, member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley). If the section is allowed to stand I shall consider the amendment.
Mr. MeKENZIE. In subsection 1 of section 5, there is an ambiguity, I am afraid, in the last line and a half. The section reads:
The commissioners shall have the power of summoning before them any witnesses, and of requiring them to give evidence on oath, or on solemn affirmation if they are persons entitled to affirm in civil matters, and orally or in writing, and to produce such documents and things as the commissioners deem requisite.
That section would serve its purpose better if it stopped with the word ' re-, quisite,' But it goes on:
Requisite to the full investigation of the matters into which they are appointed to examine.
That might refer to their original appointment as a commission or to their appointment to inquire into some specific matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that probably the point is well taken, and that the last part of the section would be implied.
The amendment probably enlarges the powers of the commission.

Would it not be clearer if it were worded:
As the [DOT] commissioners deem requisite for the full investigation of the matters then under inquiry.
' Matters into which they are appointed to examine,' is not good drafting at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it will be better to pnt a full stop after 1 requisite ' as suggested by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). I am inclined to think as it stands it is not at all objectionable.
Did the minister hear the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did. That was practically my own suggestion.
It is just changing the wording, that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I want to point out that the last words of this section as it is drafted, relate to the production of documents merely, and not the giving of evidence. The commissioners have the power to cause the production of such documents and things as they deem requisite. It is documents that are requisite and not the evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There seems no reason why the scope of the section should be narrowed, and if we stop at the word ' requisite ' and strike out ' to the full investigation of the matters into which they are appointed to examine.' I think the subsection then will meet the case. Anything more after that would be by way of limitation. I think, therefore, the suggestion of my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) is a good one, and I therefore move that all the words after ' requisite ' be struck out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
On subsection 3-powers of commissioners,
Mr. MeKENZIE. I wish to express most strongly my objection to this subsection which breaks up this court of inquiry. We have heard from the Minister of Finance, and from other hon. gentlemen on that side, a great deal about the necessity of getting accurate information upon which a scientific tariff was to be based. 1 must say to the Minister of Finance that it would be impossible for him to get that scientific inquiry, or that scientific result from the court of inquiry proposed to be established under subsections 3 and 4. Section 4 of the Act enumerates a great many things into which the court may inquire, and then under subsections 3 and 4 the commission can be split up into a number of subdivisions-not more than three because I understand there are to be that number of commissioners-any one of which may hear evidence apart from the others, and then they are to get together and they are to evolve a scientific result from the evidence obtained in that way. Now I submit to Die minister in all honesty that the kind of court which he proposes to _ establish under this Act is a gypsy institution which will not give the good results which he anticipates. In the judicial courts of the land three judges must sit, and when they hear evidence they are to notice the demeanour of witnesses. But the commissioners in this matter will have to deal with a greater matter than most of our judges have before them. They will have to deal with the whole tariff of Canada involving millions upon millions of money

to the people, and, therefore, this court of inquiry is as important, if not more important than any court we have to-day. If it would not be tolerated for one moment that a court consisting of three judges could be split up for the purpose of hearing evidence here and there, and then coming together to agree upon a result, why should such a procedure be adopted in this case? I submit to the minister that notwithstanding any further expense that might be involved to the people, and the difficulty or inconvenience which might be caused to the commission, he should as far as possible insist upon these three commissioners sitting together and hearing evidence, and that they be not split up every which way and proceed according to what seems to me to be a rule of thumb method. We heard from the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day that after travelling over this country, that after a great deal of toil and labour, he had at last to sit down in his office and give this country a tariff by rule of thumb. Now, I submit that what is proposed here is the worst possible rule of thumb procedure, and I again urge upon the Minister of Finance not to divide the commission in the way proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Cape Breton is to be congratulated on coming so rapidly towards an appreciation of the necessity of this commission.
My remarks do not warrant that interpretation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman argues that not only are the duties of the commission to be important, and not only is it vital that they hear witnesses and get evidence from all the sources they can, but he says it is even necessary that each of the commissioners be present in order that they may properly value the personal element in the evidence. So that those factors being also essential in the mind of the hon. gentleman, I am sure he sees that the objects to be served by the commission more than warrant its appointment.
What I said was that if we are to have this commission at all, if it is to be forced upon us, let us have the best possible commission. I am not saying that I want it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sure that any one who reads the hon. gentleman's remarks in ' Hansard ' will see that I quoted the hon. gentleman accurately and have made my point.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What about yourself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We want a commission and we -want a good commission.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The evidence to be brought forward is to be well weighed, and were it practicable within reason to have all the commissioners present at each hearing, I should deem it in a large degree important that they should be. But with the work to be done by the commission, and the limited number of commissioners, it would seem to me impossible that they can cover that work if the principle urged by the hon. member for Cape Breton were to prevail. There are thousands of items in the tariff, there are thousands of square miles of territory to be covered, there are scores of sources from which evidence can be obtained, and consequently there must be the utmost facility for division of the work consistent with doing it well. Now the Railway Commission is a body enjoying a judicial character, which this commission does not enjoy.
But even in the Railway Commission, one commissioner has certain powers, and two commissioners have very wide powers, given them, no doubt, for the very purpose under which powers are given to one and to two of the Tariff Commission under this Bill. Section 13 of the Railway Act is the section that gives individual powers to one and to two commissioners. In the case of the Tariff Commission, if all the commissioners ar.e to be present, even when a sitting is held at the furthest end of Canada, it is going to be a decided inconvenience to the public that may, for some urgent reason, desire a hearing before the commission at the other end of Canada. So, the proposal may have disadvantages even greater than its advantages. But the insuperable objection, to my mind, is, that it would render the work altogether out of proportion to the number of commissioners appointed. And no matter how many were appointed, the same objection would hold. I think the Minister of Finance has struck the happy medium.
Mr.- McKENZIE. So far, we have got along, perhaps not scientifically, but still we have got along, with ministerial tariff inquiries. And those bodies were not split up, but went as a body.

That is, two members of the Cabinet went, and tliey did the work for fifteen. Then I cannot see why at least part of the work could not be done by one Tariff Commissioner for the three. The bon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) seems to be still labouring under the apprehension that this commission is to have executive and administrative powers. On the contrary, this commission is for the purpose

of investigating and reporting, and that alone; and, (that toeing the case, the hon. gentleman wilil see that two commissioners, or even one, in the majority of cases, is quite competent to make the investigation. It might, perhaps, toe better that the three should hear the witnesses, observe the demeanour of those witnesses, and so on, tout the' object to he gained, is not worth the objections that there would toe to it.
On section 5, subsection 4:-
IWo commissioners shall have power to conduct any inquiry under subsections 3 and 4 of the next proceeding sections, and may, for the purposes of such inquiry, exercise the power conferred upon the commissioners by subsections 1 and 2 of this section.
Would the Minister of Finance please explain just the effect of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In cases of inquiry to ascertain whether there has been a combine to unduly enhance prices, it wias thought desirable that there should be at least two commissioners. My hon. friend pointed out the importance of an inquiry of that kind, and we thought that it should be safeguarded, toy having at least two commissioners. I think that under the 'Bailway Act, two commissioners form a quorum, and can hear causes. It seems to me that in this case, there should toe two, instead of one. Subsection 4, to which reference is here made, covers inquiry into matters referred to the commission by the Governor in Council. This is made wide in its terms-purposely wide, and may embrace very important objects', for instance transportation toy railway or by a navigation line, marine insurance, the question whether a monoply may exist in any part of the country, and so on. It .seems to us that this should be safeguarded toy a provision that at least two should he in an inquiry of that kind.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Do I correctly apprehend the Bill as to the matter which I shall now explain? The commission is to be composed of three commissioners, and under section 4' the commission is to inquire into the matters assigned to them by the Bill. By subsection 3 of section 5, one commissioner may exercise all the powers vested in the three commissioners with respect to certain matters, including the price and cost of raw materials in Canada and elsewhere, the cost of transportation, the cost of production in Canada and elsewhere, the cost, efficiency and condition of labour in Canada and elsewhere, prices received by producers, all conditions which enter into the cost of production and the price to consumers, and generally all conditions affecting production, manufacture, cost, and freight, as compared with other coun-Mr. MEIGHEN.
tries. Under section 4 these are powers given to the commission as a whole. But by subsection 3 of section 5, one commissioner alone is given power to investigate these matters. Then, under subsection 4 of section 5, you say that with regard to combines, to go no further, two commissioners, and not one, must investigate. I thought that at first the intention of the Bill was that in these matters one commissioner or two commissioners, as the case might be, should investigate, and then that the facts should be digested by the three commissioners and a report made to the Minister of Finance by the commission as a whole. But as I understand the Bill as explained by the Minister of Finance now, one commissioner or two commissioners may report to the minister on the subject which they have been empowered to investigate, and therefore, you will not have the benefit of the three commissioners in such cases. I do not think the Bill can be read otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will look at section 4, he will see that it provides, ' in respect of goods produced in or imported into Canada the commission shall, under the direction of the minister make inquiry,' and so on. Under the interpretation clause, ' commission ' means the Tariff Commission provided for by this Act. This commission is to make inquiry and report. Now, under subsection 3 of section 5, one commissioner shall have power to make inquiry into matters covered by subsections 1 and 2 of section 4, and, for this purpose may exercise the powers conferred upon the commissioners * by subsections 1 and 2 of this section '- section 5. Now, subsection 1 of section 5, gives the commissioners power to summon witnesses to testify and produce documents, and under subsection 2 of section 5, they are given the same power to enforce the attendance of witnesses and to compel them to give evidence as is vested in any court of record in civil cases. As I read the Bill, the Tariff Commission shall make a report. But we go on the analogy and in accordance with the practice of the Railway Commission, one commissioner being appointed to take evidence. Let me point out how that works out practically. There are several thousand commodities embraced under the tariff. Unless we make a provision of this kind it would be impossible to make any headway with a revision of the tariff. An inquiry may be going on in British Columbia or Alberta while another is going on in Nova Scotia.
It seems to me it is a common sense provision. It simply means that the commission must go to all (these places and give a hearing, or obtain evidence in

some other way. What we propose to do is to multiply the commission, and I think my hon. friend will see that, as I have pointed out, the matter is well safeguarded. The report of the sub-commission will be made to the commission, and while we are giving one commissioner power to take evidence, his evidence will have to be submitted to the board to be passed upon.
He reports the evidence back to the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

1 desire to ask the Minister of Finance if this Bill provides for an investigation into Ithe capitalization of bonds, into the value of the common stock, into the valuation of the physical assets of any ' company ?' According to my reading the Bill does not go that far, it does not contain provisions sufficiently wide to enable the commission to investigate those matters. I think the Bill should provide for that, because there are certain interests that are, perhaps, seeking favours from the government, for instance, the Steel Company, and other corporations, and I think it would be well to have these matters thoroughly investi-' gated so that all the facts may be laid before the commission and before parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The primary purpose of this Act in appointing the Tariff Commission is not to investigate the matters referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Sharpe); but so far as those matters have any bearing at all upon the cost of production-and they have a very important bearing upon the cost of production -then, of course, they would come within the scope of the commission, under section 4.
In what way would they have a bearing upon the cost of production?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend can scarcely be serious in suggesting that they might not have a bearing upon the cost of production. Take, for example, the cost of the production of steel; if it was important that we should know the cost of the raw material and of transportation, that is to say, the cost of raw material laid down, is it not important that we should know what capital is invested in a particular business, in order to ascertain what the real cost of production is ? Does my hon. friend mean to suggest that the cost of production does not depend to some extent upon the amount of bond issue upon fixed capital ? Is it not ia factor in connection with ascertaining the cost
of production? In order to ascertain the cost of production of steel to-day, not only what I have said with regard to raw material should be considered, but we should also know, in the case of a particular company, what is its bond issue, how much did its bonds sell for, what aTe its fixed chargee.
In that event, then, the capitalization, the bond issue and everything belonging to a company in that line, would enter into the investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No question about it at all-that is, your fixed charges, that is, your bond issue, what interest is paid. Then in addition, you have your cost of labour and cost of management; and then the question arises how much capital is invested, to what extent is the stock watered, or if it is watered at all.
Then it might take cognizance of an over bond-issue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The commission has power to go into that to ascertain the cost of production-as I have said, to ascertain what is your fixed charges, how much is your bond-issue, how much have your bonds sold for, what is your interest charges in the course of a year. Then you have the expense of management and the overhead charges as they are called, insurance, &c. Then the question arises how much capital was put in, in the case of an ordinary individual putting in a certain sum of money.
Take an analogous case, that of a railway company; does the bond-issue or the stock-issue enter at all into the computation of operating expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If you were pursuing an inquiry as to whether the freight rates, for example, were reasonable or unreasonable, does my hon. friend mean to suggest that we should not take into consideration the bonds, the interest on which must be paid first?
But your Bill does not provide for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It provides for it in the widest possible manner. My hon. friend will see that section 4 covers all that, as I explained when section 4 was under consideration, * the cost of production in Canada and elsewhere.' All these are pertinent facts. And as I say, in the case of an individual who is producing a commodity of a certain kind, you will show in addition to his own services, and in addition to the cost of labour, and to any fixed charges, how much capital he has in this

business, and what would be a proper or normal profit on that capital.
Then the cost of production would vary according to the bond-issue in two analogous companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not necessarily, because one might have a much larger output than the other. All these are questions of fact that the commissioners, in pursuing an inquiry as to the cost of production of a particular commodity, would have to inquire into, and obtain all the information available, in order to make a finding to show what is the cost of production of any commodity in Canada. All these factors will undoubtedly have to be considered in the inquiry.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It seems to me my hon. friend has not answered the point of the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe). The cost of production cannot be extended to all the points he has just stated. It is obvious that the cost of production depends upon general conditions which affect all parties who are producing in a certain line. The fact that one man has put more water in his stock than another, or the fact that one has been imprudent in his bond-issue and another has been prudent, does not at all affect the cost of production. But the cost of production is regulated by general rules.
Might it not affect the price to the consumer ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not think it can. It can affect the profits of the man who has put his money into the business. But the cost of production is regulated by general rules, which will have to be regulated here. The cost of labour, for instance, is general, so is the price paid in interest on the money markets of the world.
I think it would be proper that these matters should be considered whenever they do affect the cost of production. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for North Ontario should be included in the Bill as matters for the Tariff Commission to investigate. But I do not see how the imprudence of one man, because he does not administer his business properly, can be allowed to affect the cost of production, whenever he comes before the commission and asks for an increase in the tariff on his commodity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think my right hon. friend and myself are in disagreement at all. All the factors that have been mentioned undoubtedly enter into the cost of production. But if you have an inquiry into the cost of production, it is obvious that you must consider, among other things, the particular things mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Sharpe). 1 Mr. WHITE (Leeds).

Suppose under the Bill, if it goes into effect, the commissioners were to undertake an inquiry into the watered stock, or otherwise, of any concern, and the manager or the president of the company refuses to disclose the facts, and says, it is none of your business; I would suggest to the minister that in a case of contempt of court the minister should have more extended powers to enable him to go into that inquiry. It is extremely questionable if there is anything in the Act that would enable him to ascertain the conditions of the company. But if the minister is so clear in his mind that he has that power, why not put it in the Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You cannot put anything of that kind in specifically without limiting it. As clause 4 is drawn there are the widest possible powers given, and if you attempt in any way to limit it you fetter the commission. Clause 4 as drafted enables the commission to inquire into every factor that enters into the cost of production and, without question, the matters mentioned by my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Launer) and the matters mentioned by my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe! are factors entering into the cost of production. I surely do not understand my light hon. friend to suggest that fixed charges are not a factor in the cost of production. Supposing an inquiry is to be made we will say, into the cost of steel, that investigation must take in all the companies which are manufacturing steel. It is true, as the right hon. gentleman has stated, that one might have sold their bonds more prudently than another, that one might have a larger bond issue than another, that one company might have no watered stock, that another company might have watered stock and that a company might have watered stock to a certain amount and stock not watered to a certain amount. These are facts that must be considered by the commission and they must apply their best judgment to the facts in order to form a conclusion as to what should be a reasonable figure at which to place the cost of production of steel in Canada. I pointed out at the time I introduced this Bill that the determination of the cost of production has not been reduced to a science. You may have in one country a cost of production different, from the cost of production in another country, and you will have in the same country a difference in cost at different places and different times in the year. These are all factors entering into the situation, and they will all have to be considered. The fact that there are so many of them should not preclude the commission, or a commissioner, from investigating them. They have to consider all these matters and they have to consider them in order that they may make their finding as best they may

The argument, I have always understood, is, that watered stock, the selling of stock at a discount, and the selling of bonds at a discount, are undesirable, because they do in the end affect the cost to the consumer. If they do not have that result, they are of no importance. Therefore, if you have not only the cost of production, but the .price to the consumer to be inquired into, it is perfectly obvious that the considerations which have been mentioned by my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) and hon. gentlemen on the other side, are within the scope of the inquiry which these commissioners may make.

I would like to suggest that the hon. memiber for North Ontario draft an amendment and submit it to the committee. I think it is a matter that is hardly covered by section 4. It is possible that a general inquiry into the capitalization of a company might not come within section 4 and, at the same time, as the Minister of Finance states, it is quite possible that the commissioners could conduct an inquiry to a certain extent into the matter of capitalization. There are two schools of thought upon whether capitalization has riefeirenoe to the cost of production. Some siay that it is not an element in the cost oif production, but that it is an element when you commence to consider what profits isball be added to the cost when once determined. However,	I just rose to	call the
minister's attention again to subsection 3, of section 5. It is suggested bv my right hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, that it is hardly clear whether the commissioner would report to the minister, or whether the commission itself should report, after having the findings of the commissioner. I was going to suggest to the minister this amendment, although I am not quite satisfied with it myself:	After
the word ' power ' in the first line, you might add the words ' on behalf of the commission.' It would then read:
One commissioner shall have power on be-hr.lf of the commission, &e.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look at section 4, I am sure that he will agree that it covers the point. It says that the commissioners shall report to the minister. In other words, the commission, in ascertain-Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
ing the cost of production, would say to the man referred to by my right hon. friend: You claim that you should make 5 per cent or 6 per cent, or 8 per cent or 10 per cent, us the case may be, upon your capital stock issued, so we desire to find out how much of your capital is actually bona fide capital, and how much is water.
