Who would report under subsection 3, one commissioner or the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My intention is that it should be the commission.
I know that is your intention, but does it say so ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For the purpose of getting the best results I believe it is necessary to divide up the work.

I approve of the division of the commission.
On section 5,

The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that whatever evidence would be obtained would be fully reported to the House although the Minister of Finance was not so explicit in his statement in reference to that, but sections 5 and 6 are closely interwoven and they provide for the taking of evidence which may not be submitted to the House. I do not think it proper that this commission should take secret evidence, I believe that this commission should give publicity to every kind of evidence that is submitted to them, and that nothing should enter into their consideration which would not be open to the public and open to parliament. I do not think this proviso for secret evidence is in the best interest of the country or in the best interest of the Department of Finance itself. During the fifteen years that Mr. Fielding was at the head of that department he refused to have anything to do with secrecy of any kind, everybody had to lay his story before him open and above board, and I think that practice should be followed. I move, seconded by Mr. Charlton, in amendment:
That it shall be lawful for the commissioners to hear any application secretly or to receive in writing any representation that is not to be made a publio document.
In my opinion, there should be no objection to publicity being given to everything in the shape of evidence that is submitted to this commission. If the word * unlawful ' sounds harsh, the minister can substitute another word which will carry out my meaning, which Is, that everything pre-

sented to the commission in the shape of evidence should be made public.
I would think that probably under subsectioin 4 they could obtain evidence in any way they pleased and that section 5 is not necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One section provides that they are to make inquiry, and the other provides for the procedure. It appears to me that all sources of information should be open to the commissiqp.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: One section refers to the subject matter of the inquiry and the other provides the method.
The purpose of this section is to relieve the commissioners from the necessity of taking evidence under oath.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and to obtain a great deal more information than could be obtained otherwise. This commission will have to accumulate a great deal of information, and they can collect that information from trade reports and all available resources. Then again, they might have to get information in a foreign country and we could not authorize them to compel the attendance of witnesses in such a case.

If the idea is to apply this section only to foreign countries, I would have no objection, but in that case you have put this power in the wrong section.
Mr. WHITE, (Leeds). For instance this commission might have an accountant go into the affairs of a company and make a report, and the figures would be submitted' and it surely ought to be open to the commission to act upon that information. Now, if you had a bureau, as has been suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite, instead of this board, your bureau would have to obtain information * otherwise than by oath and affirmation, and they would act upon it. If a bureau would mean anything in connection with the Department of Finance, the Minister of Finance might act on the information obtained by that bureau no matter what source it came from, if the bureau deemed it authentic. There is, in this respect, no difference at all in principle between the two, except that this commission has very much wider powers. This being the case, I cannot >866 what possible objection there can be to subsection 5. My hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie), is looking at it entirely from a judicial standpoint; he seems to have the impression that this commission should not take evidence in any other way than under oath, but my idea is that it should very sparingly resort Mr. McKENZIE.
If you attempt to restrict it you limit the powers of clause 4 which covers everything in respect to the factors relevant to price, cost, conditions of labour and all the conditions affecting manufacture or production in Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend is perfectly right in what he states as to the object of the commission being to investigate all things that tend to disclose the cost of production. No one doubts that, but the point raised by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) is as to whether the powers conferred by the commission would authorize the commission to investigate the facts stated by him. For instance, a company may come asking for an increase in the tariff. They insist that the cost of production is much more than it is supposed to be by the commission and, desiring to give their reasons for that stand, the commissioners may say:	Very well,
let us look into the cost of production. We find you have put no capital into this enterprise, that it is all watered stock; you have given to the public a large amount of stock in which there is not a dollar but which is all water, and the company might very properly say: This has nothing to do with the cost of production.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has a good deal to do with it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, it has nothing to do with the cost of production at all. Now, the company might have a million dollars of that stock. That does not affect the cost of production one iota, and it is quite evident that the object set forth by the hon. member for North Ontario is not served by this Bill. I do not think it is quite clear that the Bill would provide for such a condition. I speak all the more advisedly upon that because the other day upon a Bill which came before this House- I do not want to refer to a past debate, but merely to mention it-we saw how particular we must be when it comes to the interpretation of a statute.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Under subsection 2 the minister clothes his commission with the procedure of a court, but under the section we are discussing he deprives them of that procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It merely provides that it is permissive to the commission to take evidence under oath if they so desire, or to act upon evidence not taken under oath if they deem it advisable.
I think under subsection 4 they could obtain evidence in any way they pleased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If that is so, what harm is there in defining what they may do, so as to make that point clear should any question arise. In reply to what was said by my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie), that my predecessor in office would not hear any confidential information, I may tell him that there is no office in all the departments of the government in which there has been more confidential informa-ion confided to the minister, and properly so, than in the Department of Finance. The Minister of Finance is the repository of the business secrets of a great many people. The Minister of Finance meets with all kinds of business people continually, and communications of the most confidential nature are necessarily and properly made to him. My predecessor, and his predecessor before him, were placed in that position time and again. There are hundreds of confidential communications on the files of my office. Now, suppose we had a bureau instead of a commission, and suppose that bureau obtained information as to the financial standing of a company or a firm, or the trade secret of a firm, or the names of customers of a firm, or the trade connections of a firm, does the hon. member suggest "that such information should be made public? I do not believe that public opinion in this
country would for a moment approve of a commission that would pry into business secrets, and make them public.
Why should we want information of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because we need all the information we can get, and if we have not a provision of this kind in the law we will deprive ourselves of information which we would otherwise get. It is quite possible that the financial standing of a firm might be in a precarious condition at the time the inquiry was being made, and would any one assert that that foot should be made known to the public ?

Might not this commission consider and act upon certain information, given to it as confidential, without it being so stated in the Bill. What authority is there to compel this commission to disclose confidential information, either to parliament or to any one else. Of course, I agree with the general argument of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe it valuable to have such a provision in the law, because I believe it will encourage people to give information which they would not give unless they knew they were protected under the statute. It seems to me that the more it is looked into the more the value of that particular subsection will appear. Prima facie, it would seem to be open to objection, but the fact is that confidential information, of the nature referred to here, has been continually placed before the Minister of Finance, whoever he may have been, and has been continually acted upon. This report of the Tariff Commission should be sent on to the office of the minister, with all the information, and if there is any statement which is in its nature confidential, that would injure a firm either in its credit or give its competitors an unheard advantage, then I think, following the usual practice and the precedents which they have held in the past, that that information should not be made up in such a manner as to injure that firm.
I think on looking at the section itself the minister will agree with me that the discretion is not with the Finance Minister, but with the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

The subsection does not say that the Finance Minister shall make the information confidential. Is not (this the great objection to the clause: That the commission may be basing their report and taking such action nnder subsection 5, and yet not one particle of that information be

given to the Finance Minister under this Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. we think not.

Yes. Under this subsection they may get such information >and use it and act upon it, and yet there may not be a particle of that in the records submitted to parliament, and parliament would have no knowledge of , the information upon which these 'commissioners have acted. Now it does seem to me that the evil of leaving these commissioners to act upon information of a private character, which is not to be communicated to parliament, is very much greater than eliminating the clause altogether and simply providing that if there is information of a confidential character the commissioners shall not take it at all. Any evidence that the commissioners may take, either under oath or otherwise, should form a part of the public records of the country, so that parliament -and the country generally can judge of the wisdom, or unwisdom, of the conclusion which they have reached from the information submitted to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) will look at section 4 he will observe that the commission has to make inquiry and report to the minister. Not only .must it report to the minister, but if he will look at subsection 5 he will see that
Inquiries under this section shall he conducted in a summary manner and the respective reports to he made pursuant to its provisions, accompanied by a copy of the evidence, if any, taken in connection with the inquiry shall succinctly state the result thereof.
They can hold back all confidential information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it does not say so.
Could they not hold back anything which they have taken orally ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They must give the results of their inquiries. In other words you must trust the commission with a certain amount of discretion. They could not pass on all the oral evidence they heard. We must look at this matter from a practical standpoint. They could pass on any evidence which they heard, but I imagine they will hear information on a great many things which it will not be possible for them to pass om. However, all this information will come to the minister. In other words, what I would like the House to understand in regard to this Bill, at least as to our conception of it, is this: that the situation is not changed radically at all. I have pointed out to the House that the Finance Minister to-day 'acts on Mr. PUGSLEY.
information which he has on file in the department obtained from a man or two that he has there, and he acts upon information obtained from deputations that interview him from time to time, and he has in addition to that a very great deal of confidential communications in his office which unquestionably influence his mind in connection with tariff matters. I think I can Tecall one budget speech of my predecessor relative to the Tariff Commission going out to take 'evidence, in which he says a great deal of the evidence is given ex parte, that a good deal of it is tinged, so to speak, and evidence that he would not altogether care to rely on; but, at the same time, a very great deal of evidence of a confidential nature did come to him, as it comes to every Minister of Finance, 'and influenced him unquestionably in coming to a conclusion on tariff matters.
If subsection 5 were struck out altogether would it make any difference to the Bill? Would not the commissioners have the same power?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Except this: while to my hon. friend's intelligence, clause 4 may seem wide enough, he is a lawyer-
No he is not a lawyer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well if he is not a lawyer he ought to be one.
Just simply a common farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If there is any doubt whatever-and there may be a doubt -then they have this specially mentioned power of summoning witnesses and any other mode which might be employed. Therefore I see no harm in having section 5 in for the reason it is to supplement the other provisions. In addition to obtaining evidence under oath they may obtain it in a mode they deem proper so long as they believe the' evidence is authentic. Now with regard to confidential information. As I have said, the Ministers of Finance in the past have acted on all classes of information, and when they have come down to parliament with a tariff they have had to prove their case as best they could, 'they would give, I have no doubt, certain facts of which they were sure, which they had obtained in such a manner as they might be able to, in order to substantiate whatever tariff changes they proposed, but confidential communications in their office were never brought down, and the practice under this would be in no way different. All this information will come into the Minister of Finance's office and will be departmental papers precisely as it would be departmental information in the case of the suggested bureau. Now upon a return be-
35(i9

ing called for by this House the information would be brought down in precisely the same way as it would be brought down in the case of a bureau. If any confidential information was obtained by the bureau or by the minister that information would not be brought down, has not been brought down, and should not be brought down.
Why have the clause in, you are only making trouble for yourself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My answer to my hon. friend is this: it is desirable to encourage people to give information' helpful to the commission. Now if this provision is not in the Act the fact will be known and, therefore, men will not be as certain of their ground as they would be if the requirement were there. Now my hon. friend approves of the principle and I understood him to say he did not see any harm in putting something in the Act to show the business men clearly that they will be protected, under the provisions of this Bill, if they give information which in its nature is confidential, the publication of which might injure them in some way. It seems to me there can be no possible objection to that.

Will the minister tell me what this section means when it provides that the information shall not be made public by the commission in such a manner as to be available for use by any business competitor or rival? Does the minister say that information shall not be brought down to parliament? Is that what he intends by that provision? He has told us about the different Finance Ministers and the information which they received. Everybody knows that Ministers of Finance receive information in regard to matters of public welfare and this is made a matter of record; and it appears on file in the department, and I have never yet heard any Finance Minister in my short parliamentry experience refuse to bring down any papers relating to the public business of the country.
Mr. Fielding refused to bring down letters on the subject of reciprocity.

They were private communications, not dealing with matters which come within the purview of what we are discussing here. Suppose that any public body interested in the tariff sent a delegation here to wait upon the Finance Minister, and they put their statement in writing and it became a matter of record. That would be all right, but can it be argued that parliament should abandon its right to have before it the information upon which the government acted, unless 113
it was of such a confidential character as comes within the well defined rules of parliamentary practice?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it is in the practice not only of the Department of Finance, but in other departments of the government not to bring down certain information.
That is well understood.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: On confidential matters.
Within the well understood parliamentary practice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And in respect to matters with which parliament has to deal.
That is well defined by all the books on the subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: For example-one of hundreds of illustrations that might be given some portions of the correspondence relating to the construction of the National Transcontinental were not brought down to parliament in the first instance, though the information was moved for. I am not criticising the action of the government of that day in that regard, but simply giving this as an illustration. The correspondence was brought down subsequently.

If we have a well defined railway rule to which we can resort to understand parliamentary practice in this matter and know what is confidential in its nature, and if it is proposed by this section to extend that in any way-the Minister of Finance says that it is not. Then, why put it in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The object is that business people and others giving information may feel certain that they will be protected. As between government and parliament there is no change under the Bill. But, if there were no such rule as this, based upon common sense and experience, that confidential communications should not be brought down, the effect would be that there would be no confidential communications and the Minister of Finance and the government would be denied information that might be of the greatest possible value. Take the. case which has been instanced of a deputation coming, presenting their views and handing in a memorandum. That memorandum becomes public property and would be brought down to the House. But suppose the minister says to one company that has been a party to it: I would like to know your financial position. Or suppose that in supplementing the memorandum a company should write giving its balance sheet and saying: You see we are in a precarious condition. But if they indicated by marking the letter ' private ' or * not official ' that they did not

desire these the facts made public, then, under the unvarying rule, such a communication would not be brought down. This Bill does not effect any change in that respect. This commission is merely ancillary to government for the purpose of obtaining information such as up to this time we have obtained in another way, and, therefore, we make it subject to the same rule that has always prevailed with regard to confidential communications.
Does not this subsection 6 provide that the commissioners themselves may suppress sworn testimony-
It says they shall not make it public.
Is not that the same thing? What, then, does it mean? It means that they shall not transmit it with their official report.
Does not section 4 control that, in. its provision that the commission shall report to the minister?

But this subsection 6 of section 5 qualifies that when it says that certain evidence or information ' shall not be made public by the commission,' as by sending in their report they would make it public.
Section 4 provides that all evidence shall be reported; and it does not confine it to evidence upon oath, or even to verbal evidence.
But, on that point, this subsection 6 of section 5 refers to ' evidence or information.' That distinguishes between evidence sworn and information given otherwise.

If it is information that cannot be called evidence of any character, then, it does not come under the provision regarding the reporting of evidence under subsection 5 of section 4. But all information or evidence must be reported by the commission. Unless that is qualified, of course, it carries its weight throughout the Bill. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) argues that subsection 6 of section 5 qualifies that and authorizes the commission to subtract from the report to the minister such information as may be confidential. But the Bill does not say that. It says the commission shall not make public that part of the inquiry that is confidential. That does not say that it shall not be reported to the minister. But the commission, in the very hearing of the testimony might make it public, and might be compelled to make it public unless released from that obligation by subsection 6 of section 5. That subsection authorises them to refrain from making public ; Mr WHITE (Leeds'
evidence of that character, but does not release them from the obligation of reporting it to the minister. The minister must get it. Then, when it has reached the minister, it is in exactly the same position as other communications that come to him.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) say that the report of this commission is in the same position as a private letter received by the minister?
In this respect, it is. The situation as between minister and parliament is altogether unchanged.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the minister having received a report based upon sworn testimony, can refuse to bring that down to parliament, because he thinks it confidential.

I have not said that. But I say that if the minister could have refused before, he can refuse now. As between the minister and parliament matters are in the same position as if there were no Bill. And it has been the practice that the minister receiving communications and reports is the judge of what is confidential and what is not, and what he deems confidential, does not come down to parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not forget
I do not forget the speech of the Minister of Finance on this point

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But he forgets that when we were on section 4, an hon. member moved that the commission, instead of reporting to the minister, should report to parliament, and then it was stated that what came before the commission would toe brought down to parliament.
Mr. MEIGH0N. Subject to this limitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I mentioned that specifically.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
One can well understand that if one communicates with a minister he has the right to set the seal of secrecy upon his communication. That is obvious. But the Minister of Finance has referred several times to the fact that we on this side were satisfied with a bureau of statistics. So we were. But he was not; he wanted to have a commission; and, as I understood it, this commission is intended to be a court for collecting evidence.
Then if the court is to receive evidence, and if any man comes before the court to give evidence, he should be told: What you say here shall not be treated as eon-

fidential; if you don't want to have it published to the world, then don't give it at all. This commission, if it is to serve any good purpose, is to collect information, not for the minister alone, but for parliament also. You are arguing now that the commission may collect information which the minister may keep to himself, and not disclose to parliament. I do not think that is the way the commission should proceed. Anything that is given to the commission ought to be given to parliament.

I do not think the point raised by the right hon. gentleman is the same as that raised by the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), w'hich I have answered, namely, that there is no restriction whatever which would relieve the commission of their obligations to report to the minister. As to the point raised by the right hon. gentleman, he says that inasmuch as parliament sees fit to appoint a commission instead of a statistical bureau, and the commission is in the nature of a court of inquiry, that necessarily evidence given before it to be transmitted to the minister is to be laid before parliament. Now there is nothing that should be public property that will not be public property after this Bill goes through. Every such piece of information presented to the minister before without the medium of a commission that was public property, and that was presented to parliament, will still be public property. Then the question arises: Is it advisable to give the commission power to go beyond that, is it advisable not to restrict the commission from investigating the private affairs of a company, and reporting that to the minister because the commission is a commission. Now that is the only question before us. If the right hon. gentleman takes the responsibility of saying that it is better to have all that shut out, that it is better for the minister to keep his eyes closed to all those facts simply because this is a court of inquiry instead of a statistical bureau, he takes the responsibility of fettering the commission.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not object to the minister's eyes being opened, but I object to his eyes being closed.

As the minister has pointed out, the course suggested by the right hon. gentleman will have the effect of closing the eyes of the minister and the eyes of every one else, because the evidence will never be given under these circumstances. There is nothing which was made public before that will not be made public now. No evidence of the character that before was necessarily 113i
public and came before the minister, will now be confidential. But it is in the public interest that the commission be not fettered from making such inquiries and such reports to the minister as are in their nature confidential, because we believe it is in the public interest to do so. I do not apprehend that there will be much evidence of this character. But it might on certain points be vital, and it is in the public interest that the minister should have it.

I object to this Tariff Commission, which is to all intents and purposes to be a court, being allowed to act upon, and to report upon, and form their judgment upon information which is not to be submitted to parliament, and of which parliament or the public is not to have the benefit. We are taking a new departure now, the majority of the House has decided that these inquiries in future are not to be made by a branch of the government, but they are to be made by an independent tribunal, whose judgment it is supposed will be the justification of- action to be taken by parliament in regard to tariff matters.
Why should that new departure affect any confidential communications?

I will tell the hon. gentleman why _ it should affect proceedings bo far as evidence is concerned. At present, if the minister makes a change in the tariff, although there may be private communications upon which he has acted, he can be questioned with regard to the information upon which he has acted, he can be questioned with regard to the exercise of his judgment, and will be obliged to give to parliament a substantial reason for making an alteration in the tariff. But in the case of an independent board, if this Bill passes, even the minister might not know the information upon which his board is acting.
The board does not act.

It does. Under subsection 5 of section 5, the board may obtain information, upon which they may act, and yet not submit it to the minister. Let me read subsection 5:
For the purposes of any inquiry under this Act, the commissioners may obtain information which in their judgment is authentio, otherwise than under the sanction of an oath or affirmation, and use and act upon such information.

According to the statement of my hon. friend, the Tariff Commission would have power to make changes in the tariff. As I understand it, they only re-

port to the minister, and it is the government that makes the changes in the tariff.
The commission would have power to report in favour of such and such action being taken, and they need not submit to the minister the information upon which they base that report.

The hon. gentleman liim

self has been a minister of the Crown, and so has the right hon. leaner ot the opposition. This Bill deals with the revenues of the Crown. Both hon. gentlemen know that the Customs Department can proceed and take evidence under oath. Information may be given relative to somebody smuggling goods into the country,' and the department may take evidence under oath with reference to that. They may fine a man, and he has no recourse, and the department need not disclose that evidence nor even the names of the witness. Even this House has no power to compel the evidence or the names to be made public. Now, this Bill is exactly on a par. It deals with the revenues of the country. It is desirable that information should be got from all sources. It assumes an old prerogative of the Crown, that the commission will have a right- to obtain that evidence; to say that that evidence must be made public, I think is going far beyond what any minister of the Crown or parliament have gone heretofore.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The two cases are not parallel at all. My hon. friend cites the case of a man who has been fined by the Department of Customs for infringing the Customs Act. That is an individual case, a direct case. Then, according to the law, the minister deals with that case, and he deals with it secretly; you cannot call for the papers under those circumstances. But here is a law which is passed, not to carry out an existing law, but to obtain information upon which to frame a tariff, the most important of all laws, because it relates to the collection of the revenue. This law is to supply general information upon which we can form our judgment as to what we should do in any individual case, what duties we should impose upon -such and such an article. That is the object of the commission, to collect evidence to enable us to form our judgment-. It is an open court to select evidence which can be digested. The two things are not at all on a par.

I think the two things are on a par. In the one case, the right hon. gentleman says we deal with the -administration of the law. Nowr complaint has been made; and no doubt the right Mr. BLAIN.
hon. gentleman knows himself how difficult it was during the last parliament to get any information with reference to tariff matters, or to the operations of the industries of the country. One of the great outstanding facts brought out last session was that the government had no information of any kind with regard to proposed tariff changes.
One of the great difficulties in connection with getting information is that, if yon establish a tribunal that has power to compel witnesses to give information, you must necessarily dig into private affairs just as much as you dig into people's private affairs when a man from the Customs Department goes into a warehouse and says to the owner:	You have goods here
that you have smuggled and we are going to fine you $10,000. He pays the money and that is the end of it. This Tariff Commission is to be empowered to go into any factory or among any class of the community for the purpose of obtaining information. For instance, it could compel the Grange to appear and it_ could question its members privately with regard to some matter concerning the farming industry. It will do exactly what the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs have always done in the past. It is simply an extension of the old prerogative on the same lines and it is a very wise proceeding. It would be very unjust and unfair to compel people to come before this commission and to give evidence relating to their private business and have their affairs published to the world.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.
My right hon. friend does not agree with me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend is altogether wrong. I would not compel any man to give evidence that ought not to be made public, and I would not give authority to these commissioners to take evidence which might not be made public.

Is not the cost of production a confidential matter? Surely you would not want the cost of production to be made known to competitors in some line of business? You nullify the whole effect of the Act unless you empower the commission to investigate into the cost of production.

Surely the citizens who have to pay the taxes that are going to be based upon tlje information collected have just as much right to and interest in a full knowledge of the information as the commission or as the government. They claim that right.

The right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) says

that he would not compel a man to give evidence that ought not to be made public. This commission compels him to give evidence. We will say that a consumer complains to the commission that there is a certain article that is being sold at a very high price and that there is a combine existing; or a purchaser might say that this combine is selling goods cheaper to his next door neighbour than it is to himself. This commission can compel everybody to appear before it and give evidence. But, if you eliminate the possibility of compelling people to give evidence, you only have oral statements and hearsay. The right hon. gentleman has been so accustomed to going by oral statements and hearsay evidence that he cannot understand how it is possible to get down to facts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has told us that the Budget was made by rule of thumb whereas Mr. Fielding never did anything of that kind. But my hon. friend will compel a man to give evidence about his business, compel him to disclose it altogether, for the benefit of the Minister of Finance who will put it in his bosom, who will not give it to me or to any of my hon. friends but who will prepare his tariff with it. We will ask him for it and he will say: I cannot give you the information. That is surely not the purpose of this commission. This commission, if it means anything, has for its object the collection of evidence which will be available to every member of parliament, nay, to every voter in this country. Unless that is the object, the Bill is not worth the paper it is written on. The object we have in view is to disseminate knowledge. I state again, as has been said by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), that the man who pays the taxes will be interested to know upon what information the law is made that compels him to pay his taxes. The commission say to a man who wants a change in tariff that he must disclose everything in connection with his business, but that the information thus secured shall not be brought before the public. On the other hand I would say to him: You are not compelled to give any evidence in this court, but any evidence which you do give shall be made public.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would simply mean that a very large and important body of information would not be available to the minister at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Possibly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is that a desirable situation or not? Is it going to do any harm if the minister or the government is in possession of information which would otherwise not be open to them, even
if the commission should resort to coercion by reason of their power of summoning witnesses and compelling evidence? My hon. friend seems to go a certain distance and then he says:	Now, stop; you must
not obtain any other information. I think he is overlogical in regard to this. How does it work out? The tariff may not be brought down to an absolute nicety. Both my predecessor and his predecessor had to content themselves with information obtained from committees, deputations and interviews. They had a great deal of confidential information, and if my hon. friend will read the speeches of my predecessor he will find that he said something like this: It has been made apparent to us, or from information we are satisfied that such and such is so. We have not had any sinister or untoward results flow from information of that kind. All we are doing is obtaining more information than possibly could be obtained under the old system by a tariff commission, and if we are also obtaining some information which is guarded by the seal of confidence we are not in any way changing the situation. The situation is precisely the same as it has been.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend what my conception of this law is. As was stated by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, this is a new departure. We used to obtain information in the way which has been stated by the Minister of Finance. The minister got it, some of it was confidential and some of it was not. But, we have now a new departure and my conception of this Bill is that it ought fo be to get information for the benefit not only of the Minister of Finance: but for every member of this parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The information obtained under the old system was not solely forth e benefit of the Minister of Finance; it was for the benefit of the government and of parliament. The information would be used in the preparation of the budget, and it would be disclosed in so far as it was not confidential. It is proposed now to gather this information in a more systematic and thorough way. Ought there to be a change in so far ad confidential' information is concerned? I cannot see any reason for any change in that regard Further than that, the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Pugsley) has spoken of the possibility of sworn information not being disclosed to parliament. What is the difference in principle as to whether you obtain that information not under the sanction of an oath or under the sanction of an oath?
It might be desirable for the considerations mentioned in this section and for other considerations not to bring it down in parliament.

Suppose evidence i,s taken in connection with the woollen schedule, and some of it is regarded as confidential and some not, then if a member moves that all the evidence taken in regard to the woollen schedule should be laid on the table, would this section restrict the right of the member to so move?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In any case, the government must take the responsibility for producing or not producing any * evidence. If parliament does not consider that the government has given good reason for withholding any information, parliament is perfectly at liberty to pass a resolution accordingly. My right hon. friend would not say that because this information is to be gathered in a more systematic way by a commission than by a bureau, that the considerations which would govern the information obtained by the bureau should not be applied to the information obtained by the commission.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But there we are establishing a board to obtain information, and if that be so the information it obtains should be public.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Is it intended that the evidence taken before these commissioners shall be open to the public or will it be a private investigation, a star-chamber proceeding? I would think it should certainly be open to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am very much surprised that my hon. friend should even suggest such a thing as a star-chamber in a country like Canada. I do not know whether he does so on account of any past experience. The hearings before the commission, I assume, will be open.
Then how can section 6 be made applicable? If the evidence is to be taken in public how could it be confidential?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Subject to the *exception in the statute.

Then the commissioners would have to know in advance that certain information of a confidential nature was about to be produced and would have to exclude the public at that point. The matters covered by section 4, the prices of raw materials, the cost of production, the cost of construction in Canada, the cost and conditions of labour, the prices receiv-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: ed by producers involve inquiries into the books of individuals, firms and companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman suggest that it should be a star-chamber?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what your argument amounts to.
No, but the moment you give the commissioners power to exclude the public while certain evidence is given under oath you make it a star-chamber inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I presume that when the inquiry approaches a point where information confidential in its nature is about to be elicited, the witness could claim privilege or the court say that the information should not be made public. The alternative would be simply a star-chamber throughout. The public would not sustain a commission which would divulge information that would injure business houses. Even in an ordinary court it- is common for a judge to receive information that is confidential.
Never.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A name for instance.
Any judge who would decide a case through information obtained otherwise than by evidence given in open court would not be discharging his duty properly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a great deal of discretion reposed in a judge. Either this information will not be obtained and consequently will not be available, or some such clause as this will have to be in the Bill. I do not see anything gained by leaving it out.

The Finance Minister stated this afternoon that the files of his department are loaded with private information which he would not divulge. There is nothing statutory to prevent him from giving out that private information and what is to prevent such private information coming to the Finance Minister in the future as in the past? My own opinion is that this commission, appointed and paid by this parliament, should report to this parliament and that all their evidence should be submitted to us. The best Tariff Commission this country has ever seen was the Tariff Commission, self-appointed in 1896.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is up to date.

The best up to date and better than this one will be in my opinion. That commission went throughout Canada

and made full inquiry into the whole business situation of the country. They did not make a decision by rule of thumb. The late Finance Minister submitted a tariff which met with the approval of the people of the whole country and for fifteen years with the approval of the present Finance Minister, the best tariff I believe that Canada ever had. I doubt very much if we can improve on it. I think it is quite proper to have inquiries made. I am not in favour of a permanent Tariff Commission.
I think it is quite well to have a Tariff Commission with ample authority to make all inquiries in regard to the trade situations of this country, but I think, Sir, that the evidence taken by that ' commission should be reported to parliament together with the commission's views on that evidence, and I think that should be made plain. I do not think that the commission should he allowed to hear evidence under oath, ox any private conversation, that is not reported to parliament. Let those gentlemen who want to make their private suggestions to the Finance Minister make them, and let the Minister of Finance keep that information secret, as has been done in the past without any statutory provision to compel it to he done. But that this parliament should authorize a commission of gentlemen to inquire into the trade conditions of the country and to take evidence and report on that evidence to the Minister of Finance without making that evidence public, I think it wrong in principle, ia<nd will be detrimental to the interests of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My bon. friend (Mr. German) has gone hack to section 4, which was debated at length the other day. Now, I think it has been stated from this side a score of times that the information that will come to the Minister of F'mance will be brought down to this House the same as any other information on record in the Department of Finance or in any other department. If there is any doubt about that I want to clear it up now. That information will be brought down. There has been absolutely no departure from the principle which has obtained in this House. If the information is in the departments here it is subject to the demand of parliament, there is no question about that. My hon. friend said why not report to parliament. Let me tell him one reason why that course should not he adopted. In the first place-as I pointed out this afternoon, and it seems to me a reason of the greatest weight-the time when the government has ito consider the question of the tariff is between sessions. There is no time in the life of busy ministers, as any hon. gentleman opposite knows who has been in the ministry, to consider such an important matter as the tariff. Now if the suggestion
of my hon. friend that the commission should report only to parliament, when would the scores of reports they should be studying and considering between sessions be available for 'the minister ? My hon. friend fails to perceive that we are working -under a system of responsible government. The government is responsible to this House and the country, and we want to -ask this Tariff Board to pursue these investigations and report to us. When tbej are made to the Minister of Finance they are made to the government. The government will have them just as it has the reports which are on file in the Department of Finance and in the other departments to-day. There is absolutely no departure in principle. There will be confidential information given. My hon. friend (Mr. German) fails to perceive it is not possible to hold 'an investigation, such as is contemplated under section 4 of this Act, into the affairs of an industrial concern, into the affairs of the commercial concern, without happening across information which in its very nature is private, which in its very nature if it were published might do considerable damage to the firm by giving a trade rival am insight into the methods of that firm which would be 'extremely detrimental to it. If my hon. friend will realize that there is -absolutely no difference in principle between the system which will obtain under this Aot and the system ini vogue 'at the present time, he will have gone far to understand this Bill and clear up his doubts in the matter. Hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon, suggested a bureau. Well, that bureau would have power to investigate an industrial plant, or a steel company, or any industry. They put accountants in, and those accountants would obtain a great deal of information. Some of that information is confidential. It is impossible to conduct an investigation by a commission without happening upon information that is confidential in its nature. It is precisely that kind of information that must be protected. It would be unreasonable to allow an investigation into the affairs of a firm if it is to be published to the world in all its particulars. If that were proposed to be done, public opinion would not justify the creation of a Tariff Commission; I think that must appeal to common sense. If my hon. friend will simply bear in mind that this is necessary to the government for the purpose of obtaining information, that nearly all the information they obtain, will be valuable, but in order to protect confidential information from publication which would do damage to those giving it, the difficulties which he seems to be afraid of would disappear, because most of them, I submit, are fanciful. The reason this provision is put in, as I have already explained, is this; it is

an additional assurance to men who have come forward and given their evidence, and who then would be quite willing that evidence should be obtained. Mr. Emery of the Tariff Board of the United States, says that men have been very willing there to give information, and that such a clause as we have in our Act is necessary, in order to protect witnesses. When a business man produces his books, his list of customers, his trade secrets and his business processes for the inspection of the commission, does any one seriously contend that all that information should be divulged to the public? I think, upon reflection, my hon. friend will see that is not a reasonable position.

Why would the commissioners want evidence under oath as to secret trade processes, and that sort of thing? Why should they take any evidence, except that which has a direct bearing upon the matters which they are there to investigate? Furthermore, why should they draw conclusions and report their opinions without the facts upon which they make the report being available for the information of parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend drew my attention to the point, because I failed to answer the argument that he advanced before. He is of the opinion that the only way that information will be obtained, will be by judicial proceedings. The commission may obtain information in a hundred different ways, and put their expert accountants into the offices of a firm to investigate. For example, one man may be making a saving in the cost of production, due to some business process, or some better method that he has over a rival, and then with regard to an industry at a critical time in the history of that industry, they would find any number of firms that were really in a precarious condition. That investigation would disclose they were nof making money, but were running behind so much every year. Now, that is information of a very confidential character. My hon. friend surely does not mean to say that the commission should publish the fact that A, B and C were in a certain line of business, were losing money, and that their business was in a precarious condition? It is surely to safeguard things of this kind that this clause is inserted, and it must be inserted, because, as I have said, the public would not permit a commission unless it were safeguarded; and in the second place, it is advisable that it should be inserted to give an assurance to business men who, knowing the subsection is there, will give information which otherwise they would not give at all. In other words, this subsection is absolutely in aid. not in obstruction, of the commission ob-Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
taining information which they would never otherwise obtain at all. I think that upon full consideration of these arguments, hon. gentlemen opposite will say that it is a necessary clause, otherwise you are forced back to this alternative: You are going to be denied a class of information that would be very useful. But you are not any further on even if you strike out this subsection. I mean to say, that, with this in the Bill, you do get the further information, but without * it you do not get that information.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), knows very well that no coercion will enable you to extort from men information, the publication of which will mean injury to their business. You might succeed in extorting some information, but you cannot get all the information you need. And you should not extort such information in any ease. It is not right. The public will stand behind this section, because it is plain business sense. There is not a man in this House who, being in business, would submit to have his whole business made known to his rivals-his better methods would perhaps have been devised by himself or have cost him money
Is there any necessity for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There might be. If there is not, the clause will not be operative. It is only to provide for a case that may arise.

The minister is assuming that some business men are going to give evidence to this commission, and through them to the Minister of Finance, which might be a detriment to their business. No man in business is going to give any information, private or public, that would be detrimental to his personal interest. The evidence he is going to give, and the only evidence he will give, will be evidence to show that he needs higher tariff protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member (Mr. German), will allow me to ask him a question. Assuming _ what he says to be true, what is the objection to the clause? If no such information is given, the clause will not be operative.
The objection to my mind is just this, and the fear is just this -that this commission is to be appointed with a view to increasing the protective tariff.
Oh, oh.

That may or may not
be true, but it certainly has a strong hold

on the minds of the people of the country that that is the object of the commission.
Is the hon. gentleman a low tariff man or a free trader?

I am in favour of fair, moderate protection to the industries of this country. But I think that the fairest protection that the industries of this country can have is 'the protection they have had for 15 years. As I was saying, there is this underlying fear that the commission may be composed of high tariff men-I am not saying that it will be; I heard the other day in Toronto who was to be the chairman, and if the information is correct, that end of the commission will certainly be on the high protection side.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he is a good man I will be delighted to tell the House, because, I am looking for a good churman.

For a good many years he was a Liberal. He is a good man, but a high protectionist. If the commissioners are all of the same kind, is it not possible for them to get private, oral evidence to make their reports to the minister on lines that will go to justify high protection? And if that is done, the ministers can shield themselves behind the report of their commission who, they can plead, have gone throughout the country and made a full investigation.
Oh, oh.

Well, I am afraid that that is what they will do; and there is a very strong feeling in the country that that is what they will do. The ministers will shield themselves behind the report, and it will be a report based on evidence that is not absolutely true to the facts, because it will be coloured by personal feeling or personal interest. There is the difficulty I see in regard to this Tariff Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman bases his case on a series of ' ifs,' none of which will eventuate.
'If 5 it does not happen all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's mind is full of suspicion. I suppose he thinks it impossible to create a fairmind-ed tribunal. I do not know his experience, but I would hate to think it impossible to pick out three disinterested, fairminded men
Who are they to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should be glad of suggestions. I do not know whether my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald,- Pictou) is
available. He is certainly a fair-minded
man, outside of politics, but when it comes to politics, he is not so fair-minded.
The newspapers say that the hon. member for York is to be one of the commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean)?
The hon. member for York, New Brunswick (Mr. Crocket).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have heard that newspapers have reported a number of gentlemen as about to be appointed on that commission. 1 have had a great number of applications. If there is any man in Canada who does not think he is fitted to sit on that commission I would like to know. I think it is possible to choose men who are not going to look at this matter from a standpoint of high tariff or low tariff, men who have a talent for economic investigation and who will regard the subject fairly. And I believe that those who want information with regard to the tariff, with regard to the dark places in the tariff, are the farmers and consumers; and I say that this Tariff Commission is more in the interests of the consumers and the farmers than it is in the interest of the manufacturers. I think it is in the interest of all. What is the purpose of the Tariff Commission?
To raise the tariff, of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purpose of the Tariff Commission is to secure information. Now, there cannot be any harm in obtaining information; you can not know too much about the facts. Our methods with relation to the tariff in the past have been hugger-mugger methods, go-as-you-please methods, rule-of-thumb methods, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said. But this government comes in with a proposal for a commission to investigate this matter and obtain information, and hon. gentlemen opposite, who can find no fault with the Bill itself-for they cannot find in it, high tariff or low tariff-declare that they are fearful and suspicious, and to justify this declaration they conjure up spectres of various kinds. They say they fear that we will appoint a high tariff commission. We have responsible government in this country, and this government is responsible to the House and to the people, and must do right or the people will hold them to account. The government will be held responsible for the appointments they make, and in the last analysis, for the work of the commission. My hon. friends opposite are a little inconsistent,^ for, 1 believe, most of them believe in this measure. And I am the first to say that

the measure should be debated because it is a departure from old methods. But now they suggest a statistical bureau. For what reason? To get information? They never made any such, suggestion until this Bill was brought down. If such a bureau was a good thing, why did not they create it five years ago or earlier? Was it because they did not feel the want of information? or because they preferred to act without information? This Tariff Commission is simply a bureau clothed with powers that could not be given to a bureau. The men appointed will be the kind of men, we hope, who will make an impartial investigation. There is absolutely nothing in the Bill which indicates that the gentlemen who are to be appointed will be high tariff men, or moderate tariff men, or low tariff men, or free traders; and anything said as to the kind of men that will be appointed is entirely without foundation, because, as a matter of fact, not one of the men has yet been selected.

Section 5 gives the commission the right to obtain information without taking it under oath, and section 6 says that any information they take should not be given by one firm to another, they need not make it public. Now, I agree that there may be a good deal of information that probably should not be made public, that is, if the commission goes into the inquiry as far as it is sug-' gested. For instance, information as to the process of manufacture should not be made public. I can imagine that there are many things people would object to say if they thought it was going to be made public. But after all, this Tariff Commission is appointed by the government, and have we a right to say that any evidence given before that commission should not be at the disposal of this parliament? I doubt it. I appreciate that there are many private communications given to the minister which he is at liberty to keep to himself; but the Tariff Commission, I think, is in a different position. But supposing these two sections 4 and 5 were stricken out entirely, would not the commission have the right to take evidence otherwise than under oath?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend must have been out this afternoon, because I have explained that many times over. Number 4 shows the scope of the Tariff Commission; it shall make inquiry as to certain specified things already mentioned. Number 5 deals entirely with procedure in obtaining information. Now, if we struck that out I have no doubt the commission might, in the exercise of its discretion, obtain the information which is mentioned in Number 4, and also keep Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
it as confidential. But I have explained why that is put in. In the first place, it is to remove a doubt, and there can never be objection to putting in a clause to remove a doubt; it is to show that they may act upon information not obtained under the sanction of an oath. Further, it is an advantage that a clause safeguarding confidential information should be in the Bill, for the reason that parties outside may be willing to give confidential information of this nature if they know that their communications will be protected by a subsection in this Act; I think these clauses should remain in the Bill.

For one, I am not yet convinced, notwithstanding that we are' feeling so good on this side of the House, that I would be willing to do almost anything to cause even a momentary pleasure to my hon. friend; but in the public interest, I do not think we should do so. I move that section 5 be amended by striking out subsection 6. I do not think it is necessary. How would it do to dispose of the amendment already moved to subsection 6?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When we resumed the sitting I had an amendment which we had considered. I think its substance is the same as suggested by my hon. friend. This amendment, I think, will add nothing to the Bill, except to make a little more clear what the hon. gentleman had in his mind. My own idea is mat the commissioners, in the exercise of their discretion, and in the conduct of their proceedings, would be very glad to give a reasonable opportunity to all who might desire to be heard, that is, to take evidence on a particular inquiry, and if any one desires to be heard, I assume they would give reasonable opportunity to parties to be heard. I think that is what the commission would do, but there is no reason why it should not be made clear if there is any doubt. Therefore, I suggest the following as subsection 2, to section 6:
The commissioners shall give reasonable opportunity to persons who may not have been so summoned to appeaT before them and give evidence upon oath or solemn affirmation as aforesaid, orally or in writing, upon any matter relating to the inquiry which is being held by the commission.
It is practically the same. My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), got very excited when he was dealing with an amendment which gave absolute right to any number of persons to come in and pile up evidence on any subject, no matter whether the commissioners were dealing with that subject or not. I do not think the hon. gentleman quite understood the situation. ' Shall take evidence of person or persons.' That simply means that the

commission would carry on its proceedings in the most desultory fashion imaginable.
My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte), said he would accept the amendment which I sent to my hon. friend. We have gained two things in Canada to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You have one or two things to your credit for Canada, I know, but they are set off against a great many other things. However, I am very glad to see my hon. friend in such good humour. He is usually in good humour, but I have not seen hon. gentleman opposite very happy for a long time:	They
looked gloomy the other day when we brought in the ' implementing ' Bill.
How is the Minister of Finance himself feeling to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is feeling fairly well, thank you.
You are not looking very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I feel reasonably well.
I wonder how the Minister of Trade and Commerce now feels about that poison which he said would be injected into the veins of the government if the election went against them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think you will find that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce is quite able to answer for himself and if my hon. friend will renew the question when he returns from Toronto, where, I believe he, is today, I think he will get an answer which will be in keeping with the ability of my hon. colleague to take care of himself. The only reason I am explaining this at some length is because the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) stampeded a little this afternoon. There can be no difference between us when I make the explanation that there is no objection whatever to a reasonable opportunity being given to persons to state their views in any particular inquiry.
That is all I want.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What I had in my mind to-day was one or ten or twenty persons coming in, offering such evidence as they might feel disposed to offer and having a perfect right to insist upon being heard. You will not find a clause like that in any statute, the railway Act or any ether. This subsection, I think will make a little clearer the intention of the Bill with respect to this matter:
Tlhe commissioners shall give reasonable opportunity to persons who may not have been so summoned to appear before them and give
evidence upon oath or solemn affirmation aforesaid, orally or in writing, upon any matter relating to the inquiry then being held by the commission.
Orally or in writing?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It follows the previous clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will put that in subsection 2.
I would like to say that I am very much satisfied with the clause as the minister has moved it. I am very glad that he is giving the people an opportunity to be heard. That is all I want.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We always intended to give them an opportunity.

In the practical working out of this matter I would like to ask the Minister of Finance how notice of the sittings or examinations or investigations into particular schedules will be given to the public? Is it the intention to publish the dates of the sittings and what will there be considered, or how will the various interests be notified? For instance, if they are going to discuss the cement schedule or the steel schedule or any such schedule will the interests be given public notice of it or in what way will the various parties receive notice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Having put this clause in I feel that very great discretion must necessarily be reposed in the _ commission. I assume that the commission will, of course, carry out their duties in such a way as is best calculated to effectuate the intention of the Bill, namely, to obtain information, and I have no doubt they will give notice of their sittings. I think that if these matters were too closely prescribed we might fetter the commission in carrying out the work entrusted to them.
If I remember correctly the last part of the amendment that the minister read stated that persons would have an opportunity ' to give evidence upon the subject under investigation '?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Upon the subject of inquiry.

I want to know to what extent that goes. Supposing, as an illustration, that they were investigating the question of the yarn duties and they were in a town away from Ottawa, we will say, in the western part of Ontario. If they were investigating that question on a particular day would it be possible for those who wanted to be heard on other questions, that they knew the commission were going to investigate later and which did not have reference to the particular line of business that they were then taking up, to be heard, because, otherwise, it would be a great

hardship. Suppose they were in Windsor, or London, and somebody wanted to be heard upon some other question; would it
be possible for them to be heard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is in the discretion of the commission.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think we could go into details of that kind in the statute. The language which has been used in that regard is the language that has been suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite-relative to the matter then under inquiry, or in relation to the matter then under inquiry. You leave it to the judgment of any tribunal as to what evidence would be relevant.

The chairman has called my attention to the fact that the record is a little bit mixed by his receiving the amendment of my hon. friend from Richmond, then my suggested amendment and then the amendment of tne hon. Minister of Finance, which is Teally the same as the one I suggested with the addition of a few words. How would it be if the amendment of my hon. friend from Richmond were withdrawn, if mine were withdrawn and the amendment of the Minister of Finance were adopted? That would keep the record right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is the correct procedure.
I do not understand what is meant by evidence ' orally or in writing.'
Perhaps it means testimony as differing from evidence. People give testimony and the evidence is the truthful part of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) will understand that evidence, of course, may be oral. But evidence by way of affidavit is written evidence.
That is never spoken of as evidence in writing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Evidence in writing would be this:	There is power taken
in the Act for the employment of experts, accountants, and so on.
You are apt to have lawyers before this commission and they will never agree that evidence in writing means an affidavit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The commission is authorized to accept any evidence that they deem to be proper. Take the books of a firm
That is never evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But it is made evidence by this Act and they may accept it Mr. NESBITT
if they see fit. Then, there are the reports of various departments of government, not only of this government but other governments, such as trade reports and everything of that kind. These do not ordinarily constitute evidence given under the sanction of oath, but, by virtue of this section it is competent to them to obtain information of that kind. What my hon. friend says is not evidence ordinarily in the courts of justice is made evidence under this Act.

If that explanation is to be accepted it is all right. I simplyr want to know if, when a man comes and places a set of- books before the commission and says that is evidence, it is to be accepted as evidence. Ordinarily it is not evidence, but if that is what the minister means it is all right.
Section, as amended, agreed to.

I wish to speak on the amendment of the hon. member. Under the present law respecting the customs, evidence can be taken on oath, and it is provided that that evidence may not be made public.	Not only is that the ease,
but the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. when Prime Minister, and his Finance Minister, Mr. Fielding, introduced what is known as the dumping clause legislation, and under that law, a number of permanent officers were appointed by the government in Chicago, Pittsburg, Antwerp, London, New York, and other large manufacturing centres in Europe and America. If it is thought that there is any dumping of manufactured articles in Canada at less than the price at which these articles are sold in other countries these officers are empowered to go into the head offices of these manufacturing concerns interested, and to compel them to show their books and to give their cost and selling prices at home and in other countries. Now, under the legislation proposed by the late government, that information is considered to be confidential and no member of this House has the right to move for a return showing what that- information is. speechtext: All these reports given in the line of what is called for, there, in getting information which is the basis of tariff measures, is the property, not of the government, or of the minister, hut of parliament and of the country. Here is another instance:	The United States Congress, not altogether a star-chamber body, not a body wholly unused to constitutional methods, created a tariff board-or attempted to do so, and would have created it had not methods similar to those used by hon. gentlemen opposite filibustered it out of the House.
