Once you make it public, it is open to business competitors as well as the whole world to make use of it.

Let us be fair and don't let ue be partisan. The1 Bill! introduced into Congress made a provision that the commission should be composed of both political parties, a certain number of Republicans and a certain number of Democrats, It was supposed to be a non-partisan commission. Unfortunately, or perhaps fortunately, in this country we do not recognize political parties as they do in the United States, where they give them a legal standing. That was the idea of the United States Commission, it was to be non-partisan. I hope that our commission will be a non-partisan commission; I only hope that the statement is true, made by hon. gentlemen opposite, that a very prominent Liberal is to be a member of the commission, and that the commission will be non partisan. Now why should that commission not stand as a buffer between the manufacturers, we will say, and a minister of the Crown? Suppose that a certain line of business in this country, say the leather manufacture, which iis supposed to be carried on largely by Liberals, was investigated by this commission', which finds a state of facts, without giving the names of the people that were investigated. If hon. gentlemen have read, for instance, the schedule on woollens and other things in the States, they would understand it. Now, if the minister was unfortunately opposed to the majority, or to some of the members of firms engaged in that business, he might take advantage of his position to pass legislation that would seriously injure them. I could name another line of business, for instance, the manufacture of iron pipe. Most of the people engaged in the manufacture of iron pipe are Liberals, and if they were investigated by this commission, and facts were brought out, which they thought it would perhaps be well to withhold from parliament, largely composed of the opposite side, this commission, being non-partisan, would simply make a plain statement of the facts, without giving the names of any members of the firms or of any members thereof. Now, if there is a buffer offered by this whole Bill to the Liberals, who are manufacturers, it is that very clause in the Bill. I do not assume that the Minister of Finance iis illiberal, but suppose 'he should be so unfortunate as to have strong partisan feelings, where would my good Liberal friends in the manufacturing Mr. PUGSLEY.
business be, if the minister could compel this commission to be constantly investigating them to find out the condition of their business, and proclaim their financial standing to the whole world, and put their business into such' a shape, that they could not get money to carry it on? I do not think there is any ground of complaint.

Before six o'clock, I stated, in answer to a question put to me by the Minister of Finance, or in some manner at least, that I believed in the principle involved in this section. What I meant was that there must be many occasions on which the Tariff Commission would be in receipt of evidence which would be considered as confidential and which would be tendered to them only upon the understanding that it is to be* held as confidential. In "the very nature of things the commission must constantly be receiving information of a confidential character, but, I believe, that confidence can better be retained by the elimination of this clause. There is nothing in the Bill itself which compels the publication of any evidence or information which comgs to the commission. If any confidential information comes before the commission, I assume it would be their duty to ascertain whether the facts stated therein were in substance true and if the commission found them to he true they could make them a part of the report of the findings of the commission. It is a very unfortunate thing to concede by statute the power of making evidence or information confidential particularly when received by a public body whose chief duty is to go around the country ascertaining information. There is nothing in this Bill compelling the commission to disclose information given to them confidentially, and it is in the interest of everybody that the commission themselves alone determine how to safeguard confidential information, permitting at the same time the person or persons tendering this information to decide as to what shall be the measure of it. I know of no other instance in legislation where a similar power was asked for. I do not think it is very important what they do in the United States in so far as the matter of the form of our legislation is concerned. I think we are very much ahead of Congress in this respect, and I do not think the fact that; there is a similar clause in the Unite;} States Bill affords any justification for this clause. I propose voting for the amendment of my hon. friend from St. John' simply because I think the restriction im-

posed by the Bill on the commission is absolutely unnecessary, and it is very much better to leave in the hands of the commission the power to determine how they shall treat confidential information.

I would like to point out to the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), that under a clause of the Bill which we have not yet reached the commission have power to pass regulations which, on being confirmed by order in council, and by the minister, become law. If you do not put limitations upon the face of this Bill the commission may pass what regulations they please. I believe that the proper way of framing a commission Bill is to make it as short as possible to place certain limitations upon their actions. That is identically the form of this Bill. It does not go into a long rigmarole and lay down in detail what they can and cannot do. This is the proper form of a Bill creating a commission. You have put a clause in permitting persons to appear before them and give evidence. Then you must also put in a clause preventing. the passing of any regulations compelling the evidence to be made public. Then, the people who come before them will know that they have that protection. This is not a question of party; there are just as many Liberals, and perhaps more, engaged in manufacturing and other business in this country as there are Conservatives. Conservatives are not the only people whose interests are going to be involved by this commission, and it is in the interests of all that these facts should remain as they are, that the Bill should remain as it is and I believe that nobody who has at heart the best interests of individuals engaged in different lines of production will support an amendment of this kind.

There is one thing that I forgot to mention. It has reference to the Congressional Bill mentioned by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen). My hon. friend also forgot to quote section 7 of the Bill which is very important as showing that the draftsman seemed to have in his mind that in some way the Tariff Board should be prevented from making evidence public in such a manner as to be available for any business competitor or rival, yet by the next section he was very careful to provide that all testimony should be available for the information of Congress. The words of the section are as follows:
That said board shall submit the results of its investigation, as hereinbefore provided, including all testimony, together with any explanatory report of the facts so ascertained to the President or to either House of Congress from time to time when called upon 114i
by the president or the leader of either house of Congress.
_ All I want is that whatever testimony is given before these commissioners who are constituted a court, shall be available to the minister, to his colleagues in the government and to this parliament. That is all we want and if my hon. friend will consent to another subsection being added similar to the one in the Congressional Bill I shall be quite willing to withdraw my amendment, and let the subsection be included. What I thought of proposing is this:
The said commission shall submit the results of its investigation as hereinbefore provided including ali testimony to the minister who shall lay the same before parliament within ten days after the opening of the next then ensuing session.
If my hon. friend will consent to that I will be quite willing to leave the subsection just as it is. If the commissioners choose to obtain information privately let them do it. Give them large latitude in that respect; I think that is a just and sound principle. But what we do want is that whatever testimony they take, with all the power that they are going to have to go from one end of this country to the other to compel people to come before them and to examine into their business matters, shall be available for the members of this parliament.
And made public?

Then parliament can deal with it as they please. If this parliament is satisfied that there is information of a confidential nature that ought not to go to the public upon the recommendation of the Minister of Finance probably a committee of this House can be appointed to deal with it. But, at all events this parliament and not this Tariff Commission, should be the judge as to whether evidence is of a confidential nature or not.
_ It is contrary to every principle affecting the public interest that this commission should have power to say that they can keep their doors open or that they can close them just as they please. It is not right to give them the power to say that when they are investigating Mr. A's business the public shall be allowed in, and when they investigate the business of Mr. B that the doors shall be closed and the information he gives treated as confidential. That is a power which ought not to be vested in this board which is practically independent of parliament for a period of five years.

Is it not the fact that in the past the Cabinet ministers have had the advantage of information which was not available to parliament and not in the public interest to disclose?

' Mr. PUGSLEY. Undoubtedly so, and they will still have that privilege. There is nothing in this Bill which takes away from the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Customs 'the power or right to receive confidential information. But, when the Minister of Finance asks parliament to make n change in the tariff he has to give the reasons to parliament for 'that change, ai d he is responsible to parliament. But that is a very different thing from constituting an independent tribunal with the power of examining witnesses undei oath and to determine what evidence shall be open to the public and what evidence shall be private.

I wish to point out to the hon. gentleman that the Congressional Bill does not give the commissioners the same power as to subpoenaing witnesses as the Bill we have now under consideration. It is true that the Congressional Bill says the commissioners shall have power to summon witnesses, but if a witness does not appear there is no remedy and all the commissioner can do is to report the fact to Congress. Under the present Bill, if the witness does not appear he is liable to imprisonment. The reasons for protecting evidence of a confidential character under our Bill are much stronger than under the Congressional Bill, because under our Bill we can put men right into the factories and take the most confidential information that their books contain. The very fact that we are giving this commission these larger powers is the reason why we should treat the information we have thus compulsorily obtained, more or less confidentially. If you are going to get at the root of the matter and you rvant to get full and frank information as to any particular line of industry, the very fact that the manufacturer knows that the information will not go into the hands of a competitor in his business will be a reason why he will be more frank about it. We have to choose in this case between an absolute publication of all the evidence as to a man's private business, or we have to put in some limitation of this kind. I would not like taking on myself the responsibility of making the secrets of every man's trade in this country absolutely open to the public. The clause of the Bill simply says that the information shall not be made public in such manner as to be available to a competitor.
What does that mean ?
I think it would permit the commission to make the evidence public to the minister and it would enable the minister to make it public to the

Cabinet Council which is sworn to secrecy. If you are at the .stage where under this Bill you can give this information to the Minister of Finance and to the Cabinet Council, are you in any different position than you are to-day as to the confidential information you receive, and which of course goes to the council 'and which may never go a step further? When that information goes to the council chamber then you can as heretofore use your discretion as to whether it should be made public or not.

But is it not a fact that these 'commissioners can determine as to when the doors can be closed and a star-chamber investigation proceeded with, or when the doors can be opened 'and the public admitted ?

There is nothing in 'the Bill which says the commissioners shall not publish the evidence. It says they Shall make a report of the fact and they snail submit the evidence, except that it -shall not -be submitted -in such a manner as- that it may be used by a trade competitor. There is no power in this Bill for the commissioners to refuse to give to the -minister the evidence they obtain; the only restriction is that they themselves shall not make public the evidence in such a manner as to be used by a competitor.
Is it not so that if this Bill passes the commissioners can determine when they can hold -secret inquiries or when they should hold public inquiries?

I do not think so; I think the minister would have the right to demand -at any time -all the evidence that the -commissioners -have gathered, but that evidence should not be made public in such a manner as that it might be used by a competitor. The minister would give the evidence to the Cabinet Council which is sworn to secrecy, and then you are in the same position as you are in to-day. You determine whether or not it is in the public interest that the information should oe made public.
It rests with the commission to say whether the evidence shall be taken in open court or whether it shall be taken in secret.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friends are too theoretical about this. How it will work out in practice is this: suppose any business man in this House is asked to give evidence on oath before the commission, he invokes the subsection which says that evidence is not to be made public in a way to injure him with a trade rival, and as a matter of common sense is there a man in this House who would seriously suggest that a business man of this country should

be subpoenaed by this commission 'and asked to divulge the last secret of his business before a crowded court room ?
The mere statement of the thing brings its own refutation. It is not to be thought ' of, public opinion would not stand for a moment for the creation of such a tribunal. It seems to me that every phase of this matter has been brought before the committee and considered. In order to enable the commission to come to a correct and proper judgment as to whether the duties on particular commodities are sufficiently high to enable capital invested in them to earn dividends, it will be necessary to go into an inquiry outside probably of the inquiries we all have in our minds at the present time. We do know that in the last two years a great many companies have become reorganized, amaigamated and combined with other companies, and in the process of this reorganization, they have increased their capital to a very large degree; they have issued bonds and preferred stock and common stock to an extent lyhich would appear to us to be altogether out of proportion to the amount of capital necessary to be invested in that particular industry. The amount of capital in a company has to do with the amount of earning power which that company possesses and the proportion of dividends that is divided from year to year among the stockholders. If the capitalization is large, the earning capacity relatively will be small. Owing to the enlargement of these companies, the presidents and directors vote themselves larger salaries than in the past. This has a bearing upon the dividends. In order that all the facts and circumstances may be before tile commission before they report to the minister, I think it would be necessary to add an amendment. I propose to add to section 5, the following subsection:

The question of capitalization of companies is a large one, and its investigation may have several objects. One object may be to ascertain whether overcapitalization affects in any way the cost of production. There might also be an investigation to see whether it affects the (banking of the country generally, or if it affects the credit of our country or of our industrial institutions abroad and so on. Only one section is to be investigated by this commission, their only object is to ascertain how far, if at all, over-capitalization affects the cost of production or affects any matter that concerns the tariff. They have no power to investigate over-capitalization in so far as it affects such other objects as I have mentioned. This. Bill already clothes the commission with all powers requisite for this purpose and requires no amendment.

I quite understand the provision of the Bill limiting inquiry with respect to the subject to be dealt with by the commission, but I desire to enable the commission to have all the facts before it, particularly when a certain industry claims that it has not sufficient protection to enable it to earn dividends. The question of capitalization is a very pertinent one and ought to be considered in connection with this matter. The wages paid to their employees and the salaries paid to their directors all add to the cost of carrying on an industry, and if they are unnecessarily high there is no reason why the capital invested in that industry should make that an excuse to have further protection to enable them to earn greater dividends.

It is the same subsection as was moved by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), excepting that it does not conflict with subsection 6. I think the Minister ought to adopt this subsection, because there really cannot Ibe any objection why the evidence which is not confidential should not be put in the possession of the members of this House at the earliest date possible after parliament meets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would be very glad indeed to take the matter under advisement if the hon. gentleman will allow the matter to stand.
If ten days is too short ia period the .time can be extended.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will consider the matter carefully.
On section 7,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would Suggest that the following be inserted after the word ' enquiries ' on line 25 of subsection 2.:

And may employ shorthand reporters.
The commission will need to employ shorthand reporters to take the evidence wthereever it may be sitting.
I would point out to the minister that from my reading of the Act the staff should come under the provisions of the Civil Service Amendment Act of 1908.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The employment given under this Act may be of a very limited character. The commission wiil have to employ different classes of men, and offhand I do not think it would be wise to put them under the Civil Service Act. The check upon employment is of course the Governor in Council.

And the reporters may only be employed for a short time.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 8-salaries of commissioners,

Are these not pretty h|gh salaries, $7,500 for the chairman, and $7,000 for each of the commissioners, in addition to all travailing expenses? The Minister of Finance and his colleagues have to serve the country for a salarv of $7,000.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Look at the honour they enjoy though.

The judges of the Superior courts of the country get I think $6,000. That is the limit, in the smaller provinces. In New Brunswick $6,000 is the salary of a pusine judge of the highest court in the province. The salary of the chief justice is $7,000. Now, it is proposed to pay the chairman of this commission a salary of $7,500, and the commissioners $7,000 each. Although the tendency of late is to give pretty good salaries to commissioners, I am inclined to think that this goes a little too far in that direction. In this country $7,000 is a very good salary. In the public departments there are men in very high positions receiving $3,000 and $4,000 a year, men who have been in the service a long time, who are charged with great responsibilities and have the control of the expenditure of vast sums of money. The deputy ministers receive only $5,000, and they hold positions of the very greatest responsibility. It may be that some more liberal allowance should be made to the public officials, but up to the present time, we have not gone far in the direction of paying high salaries to anybody but commissioners. In this case it is proposed *to follow that line and give very liberal salaries to these commissioners. I think it only fair to compare this with what public officials are receiving. The chairman of the managing board of the Interconial railway receives only $6,000. And he must 'he a man of experience, of good judgment, and of tbe very highest technical knowledge.

Under subsection 3 the matter of witness fees was brought up. I suggest that am amendment be made there and that the subsection be made to read:
All salaries and actual and reasonable travelling expenses, witness fees, and all other expenses incidental to the carrying out of the provisions of this Act shall he payable out of any appropriation granted to His Majesty by parliament to defray the same.
The addition there, is the words ' witness fees/ This insures that these fees shall be payable out of the appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will consider that suggestion of my hon. friend when considering that of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald).
If anything is to be governed by regulations surely this should be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That might be. I will consider the suggestion. Now. with regard to what my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has said: I believe that no commission that has been appointed by the government, not even the Railway Commission, will be charged with more important duties than the Tariff Commission^ a very high order of intelligence and special aptitude will he required for this work. And when we consider the scale of remuneration in recent years, the salaries paid to men in the world of business and finance and in professional life now as compared with a few years ago. I think my hon. friend will agree that $7,500 for the chairman, and $7,000 for the commissioners are not high salaries, provided we get the right men for this important work. In the Railway Commission the chairman who' As a very exceptional man and occupies a very exceptional position, and who must be a lawyer of high attainments, receives $10,000 a year. That is a very small salary for him. The other members of the board. I understand receive $8,000. The salaries of the Tariff Commissioners are placed below these figures, and I think they should be placed below, although this work is fully as important as, or even of more importance than, that of the Railway Commission. It must be borne in mind also that when you ask a man to take a position on this commission, or in faction any other commission, if he is a man in active business you interrupt the business in which he is engaged, and unless you compensate him reasonably well the offer will not appeal to him.
He has to devote his whole time to the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is provided for in the Bill. Take men of high ability and with the good judgment and knowledge required for the position, and I submit to the judgment of the House that the salaries fixed are reasonable. To be frank, I have been afraid we should not be able to obtain the class of ability I wrould like to obtain at the salaries fixed. The hon. gentleman has spoken _ of the salaries of members of the Cabinet. I think it is clearly understood, and the hon. gentleman would probably be the first to concede, that these salaries are probably the least consideration with those who take these responsible positions and give their time to these duties.
'What is the main one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is the
public service. If not, you reduce the position merely to a seven thousand dollar position. I should not like to believe that the ministers have that principally in mind. The hon. gentleman referred also to the civil .service. Since coming to Ottawa I have been impressed with the very high class of men whom you have in the civil service who are not paid nearly enough, such men as the chief engineer and other engineers. I am assuming that _ the men occupying these responsible positions have the ability to fill them, as I believe they have. Those who have been longer in Ottawa than myself can pronounce upon that point better than I can. But some of these exceptionally able men have salaries out of all keeping with the importance of the positions they fill. That is a condition whi h in time may be remedied. Of course, there may be men in such positions who are overpaid, not having the ability to fill these positions properly. One difficulty of the civil service is that it standardizes positions, as it were, and brings men to a common level. Of course, there is greater certainty in their employment, and they have a pension to look forward to, and so their future is taken care of, and they have a fixity of position that does not apply outside. But, after all that is said, I have no hesitation in expressing my own opinion that the ablest men in the civil service occupying these high positions are not well enough paid. Of course, I am not speaking for the government, but give what has struck me in my own observation and express my own opinion.

I just want to put in my earnest protest against the amount that is being paid in these salaries. In my judgment, 'there is no warrant, in the statement of the duties of these gentlemen, for the payment of this salary. The idea that men wihoise business it is simply to make the inquiry into industrial or commercial con-Mr. NESBITT.
ditions, should be entitled to the same compensation as members of this government, or members of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, or of the Railway Corn-Commission, does not appeal to me at all.
I certainly think that the salary of $7,000 each, proposed to be paid to the commissioners, who are not required to perform administrative functions nor yet judicial functions, but simply the functions of investigators, is out of all proportion to the duties they will be called upon to perform. If the civil service is underpaid, that is no reason why such a startling exception should be macle in the case of these gentlemen, who certainly cannot claim any higher rank, or sustain any more necessary qualifications for the work they have to do, than the gentlemen who are in the higher positions in the civil service. If we can properly administer an expenditure of $60,000,000 within two years, under the control of one man, who draws a salary, I think, of $10,000, then I must protest that a proposed payment of $24,500 to secure the collection of information such as suggested in this Bill, is absolutely out of proportion. To say that these gentlemen have duties that require greater abilities or experience than a deputy minister of this government, has no foundation in fact. These extraordinary salaries give this proposition the appearance of being a gross political job.

I think these gentlemen will find it very irksome business to keep tab on all their expenses from time to time. It seems to me, it would be better to give them a sufficient salary to cover once for all their travelling expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that would be impossible. We do not know how much a man will spend in travelling. In cases of this kind, travelling expenses cannot be foreseen.
On section 10, franking privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I move that this section De omitted. The Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) has a strong objection to extending the franking privilege to every one who may have correspondence with this commission. He thinks that the Post Office Department should stand on its own basis, and I am disposed to agree with him. It seems hardly fair that the post office should * be deprived of the revenue that, it needs, to carry on its business.

The franking privilege may properly be extended in respect of letters which are sent by the commissioners from Ottawa; and don't you think that those who have business with the commission, who want to make complaints, should be allowed to write to them free of postage, as is done in every other public department?

Mr. WHITE (Leeds) It is extraordinary how few people avail themselves of the franking privilege. I think a very large percentage of those who write to the departments, put a stamp on their letters for fear they will miscarry. The amount being so small, there is no hardship upon the people who desire to make communications to the commission, in asking them to pay the postage.
Progress reported.

Would my right hon. friend tell us what business will be taken up to-morrow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will take up government Bills.
Any particular one ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will take up as many as possible-I think Item 25 which would have been taken up to-day except for the absence of the hon. -member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux).
That is the Bill to amend the Civil Service Act ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. We will probably take up Order Number 21, Bill (No. 77), 'and I would hope that we may be able to take up Order Number 3, Bill (No. 97), and possibly the second reading of Bill (No. 100); after that, Supply, the estimates of the Minister of the Interior.
The Grain Act will not be taken up ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understand the Grain Act is not coming up to-morrow, but it is to come up on Monday, I think.
Might I suggest that Friday would be rather an unfavourable day upon which to take into consideration the Highway Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Why ?
There is usually a very small House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Highway Bill is not responsible for that.
I know, but it is rather an important Bill.
